chapters.title: 15 · Computing, memory, power and interface silicon
headings: 01 · Processing and computing chips — the brain
02 · Memory and storage chips — where values and instructions live
06 · Connected mental model: how a complete system works
chapters.text:
The internal architecture of digital devices, from executable instructions and volatile/nonvolatile memory to power regulation, physical buses and virtual network interfaces.
Reading key: “From the original page” paraphrases the handwritten source; “Technical expansion and corrections” is editorial explanation, not part of the manuscript. Original scans are reproduced unchanged and embedded for offline use.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook
From the original pages: The page lists CPU, GPU, MCU, TPU, NPU, DSP, ASIC and FPGA, with functions: execute instructions, perform calculations, run operating systems/software, control logic and manage execution.
Technical expansion and corrections: CPU is a general-purpose instruction executor; GPU excels at parallel workloads; DSP handles signal-processing pipelines; NPU/TPU accelerate neural-network operations; MCU combines processor, memory and peripherals for embedded control. ASIC is a custom fixed-function implementation; FPGA uses reconfigurable logic. These categories overlap: a SoC can contain several of them.
System walkthrough: A web request enters through NIC → kernel network stack → application code running on CPU; cryptography may use CPU instructions or accelerators; a GPU/NPU is used only when the workload calls for it.
From the original pages: The notes separate working/volatile memory from persistent/nonvolatile memory, listing SRAM, DRAM, FRAM, EDO, SDRAM, DDR/DDR2, GDDR, HBM and ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash/NOR/NAND.
Technical expansion and corrections: SRAM commonly implements caches; DRAM implements main memory; GDDR/HBM are bandwidth-oriented memory families. EDO is a legacy DRAM generation, SDRAM denotes synchronous DRAM and DDR is a family of SDRAM. FRAM is nonvolatile, so it must not be placed unqualified in the volatile category. NOR and NAND flash retain data without power; SSDs combine NAND flash with a controller. ROM/PROM/EPROM/EEPROM differ in programmability and erasure. Volatile memory usually loses its working state without power, but power loss does not guarantee secure erasure of every remnant.
System walkthrough: Code on SSD → loaded into RAM → CPU caches → CPU registers and execution → modified data written back to storage when explicitly persisted.
From the original pages: The page describes PMIC, DC-DC, LDO, VRM and battery-charging ICs as electrical gatekeepers that take input from wall power or batteries and distribute stable rails to silicon. It distinguishes static/base power from dynamic demand.
Technical expansion and corrections: A PMIC coordinates power sequencing, charging, monitoring and rails; a VRM is a regulator module supplying processor rails; a DC-DC converter changes DC voltage; an LDO regulates with a linear dropout stage. Power demand varies with voltage, clock frequency, activity and leakage. “Static” and “dynamic” are power-consumption components, not two exclusive kinds of regulator.
System walkthrough: Battery/adapter → PMIC and converters → regulated voltage rails → CPU, RAM, radio, SSD. Voltage stability and thermal constraints influence clock throttling and reliability.
From the original pages: The notes group guided internal PCB traces (PCIe and SATA/NVMe), guided external plugs/cables (display, Ethernet, USB, CAN), and unguided external links (modem, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth). They mention SmartNIC, DPU and NIC.
Technical expansion and corrections: PCIe is a high-speed interconnect; NVMe is a storage command protocol commonly transported over PCIe, while SATA is a separate storage interface. Ethernet MAC and PHY are distinct functions: MAC frames and addresses traffic, PHY handles physical signaling. USB controllers manage protocol transactions, and USB-C is a connector that can support multiple modes. CAN is a bus protocol. Wireless radios use RF front ends, baseband processing and antennas. SmartNICs/DPUs can offload networking and security tasks, but are not required for every NIC.
System walkthrough: Application data → OS network stack → NIC MAC/PHY → cable or RF medium → peer NIC → peer OS/application. Physical bits, frames, packets and application messages belong to different layers.
Power input → PMIC / DC-DC / VRM → regulated rails ↓ Persistent NAND / SSD → RAM → CPU caches → CPU / GPU / accelerator ↓ PCIe / USB / Ethernet controller ↓ MAC → PHY → copper / fiber / RF ↓ Linux host ↔ bridge ↔ veth ↔ container Every arrow represents a different dependency, not necessarily a direct physical wire: storage supplies persistent bytes; RAM holds active data; processors execute instructions; controllers adapt device-specific transactions; and NICs convert between digital frames and physical signaling. Kernel drivers and protocols coordinate the path.
Cross-links: See processing architectures , memory hierarchy , NIC hardware and Linux networking .

chapters.title: 18 · Computer architecture: instruction sets to distributed systems
chapters.text:
The next five pages refine the taxonomy of computing systems and cross-link earlier kernel, memory, virtualization, networking and software architecture chapters.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook
CPU ISA and microarchitecture, memory organization, hardware systems, software and deployment are distinct axes. RISC/CISC are ISA design families; x86 and ARM are ISA families, not direct equivalents to SIMD/MIMD.
Editorial interpretation and clarification of B016 page 1; original page preserved below.
Flynn taxonomy: SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD. SMP is shared-memory multiprocessing; MPP usually means many distributed-memory compute nodes. Client–server, peer-to-peer, clusters, monoliths and microservices describe different software/deployment dimensions.
Editorial interpretation and clarification of B016 page 2; original page preserved below.
Memory architecture addresses storage and access; CPU architecture addresses execution; hardware architecture connects compute, memory and I/O. UMA/NUMA can coexist with SMP; a cluster does not inherently share RAM.
Editorial interpretation and clarification of B016 page 3; original page preserved below.
Typical systems use virtual memory and caches. Cloud instance types expose a selected guest ISA, vCPU and memory topology; actual NUMA layout and locality depend on host and VM configuration. Paging does not imply that all memory resides on disk.
Editorial interpretation and clarification of B016 page 4; original page preserved below.
NUMA tuning can improve locality for databases and high-core-count servers; it is not universally required. Distributed-memory systems exchange messages across machines; Kubernetes, Hadoop and Spark have distinct execution and storage models. Shared memory supports fast local IPC but requires synchronization.
Editorial interpretation and clarification of B016 page 5; original page preserved below.
Instruction set (x86-64 / AArch64) → CPU execution and cache hierarchy → MMU and virtual memory → UMA/NUMA RAM topology → OS scheduler and processes → VM/container isolation → service architecture → cluster networking and distributed data.
These arrows indicate a conceptual dependency path, not that every category is a subtype of the next. Cross-links: memory and NUMA (B015) · process/container/node (B014) · silicon and hardware (B013) .

chapters.title: 19 · Built-in architecture, runtime tuning and deliberate distributed design
headings: Three decision layers—not three absolute categories
Technical accuracy notes (editorial, not alterations to originals)
chapters.text:
A refinement of the previous chapter: distinguish capabilities supplied by silicon and operating systems, tunable behavior on one machine, and architectures requiring multi-system coordination.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook
Layer A · Platform-provided foundations. CPU ISA and cores, caches, address translation support, firmware and the operating system's memory manager are supplied by the chosen platform. They do not require inventing an architecture from scratch, but the choice of processor, kernel, machine type and deployment still matters. Virtual memory and paging are typically enabled and managed by the OS; segmentation varies greatly by ISA and OS. UMA is not universal : some servers expose NUMA topology.
Layer B · Configurable runtime behavior. Thread placement, CPU affinity, NUMA policy, huge pages, swap policy, cache-aware algorithms, concurrency limits and workload scheduling may require deliberate tuning. Shared-memory concurrency is not automatically safe: synchronization and memory ordering still matter. Cache hardware is automatic; cache-friendly software design is not.
Layer C · Architectures that must be composed. Client–server, peer-to-peer, microservices, clusters, distributed storage, distributed memory abstractions, load balancing and autoscaling require explicit design, deployment, networking, security, failure handling and operations. Some cloud services automate parts of this, but automation does not remove architectural choices.
Edge meanings: hardware provides execution and devices to the OS; the OS exposes managed resources to applications; runtime policy changes resource use; application components communicate locally or over networks; distributed deployment adds inter-node failures, coordination and security boundaries.
RISC and CISC are ISA design families, not automatic versus manually designed architectures. SIMD is an instruction/data parallelism model and does not imply a super-scalar processor; superscalar means issuing multiple instructions per cycle. MIMD can exist inside one multiprocessor machine as well as across machines. MPP often describes large-scale parallel systems, not necessarily shared memory. NGINX and HAProxy can distribute application traffic; cloud ELB is a managed load-balancing family, and Kubernetes autoscaling is a separate resource-control mechanism. These are complementary layers, not interchangeable alternatives.

chapters.title: 20 · Processes, execution models, backup and archives
headings: 05 · Three independent ways to classify storage
chapters.text:
From a program executing as a Linux process to background jobs, deadlines, threads, and durable storage operations.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook
Source concept: “Process = running instance/object.” Technical refinement: A process is an executing program instance with a virtual address space, credentials, open file descriptors and kernel-managed resources. A thread is a schedulable execution context within a process. A process may contain several threads.
Linux connections: PID, PPID, process state, /proc , ps , top , systemctl , fork , execve , scheduling and cgroups. Compare with Chapter 19 (platform versus runtime tuning) and Chapter 16 (Linux and containers).
Your business/process note groups work into core (direct value delivery), support (HR, accounting, maintenance), and management (planning, controls, strategy). This is a business-process taxonomy , distinct from the OS-process categories above. A payroll business process can execute as a batch software process; the same word “process” operates at two levels.
Cross-link to Chapter 05 for institutions and operating models, and Chapter 06 for scheduling and operational systems. Analogy only: a department is not literally a Linux process.
Notes preserved: NAS (often SMB/NFS), SAN (often Fibre Channel/iSCSI), cloud object storage (e.g., S3 API), and archive-transfer tools such as NDMP, LTFS, rsync and SSH/SFTP. These are not interchangeable: NDMP is associated with backup data movement, LTFS with tape file organization, and rsync with file synchronization.
Connectivity: DAS, NAS, SAN. Data interface: file, block, object. Physical medium: HDD, SSD, magnetic tape. A NAS appliance can use HDDs or SSDs; an object-storage service can be built on many underlying media. These axes should not be merged.

chapters.title: 22 · From telegraph-era controls to AI-era networks, standards and schedules
headings: 1 · The common system behind all six pages
2 · Era-by-era comparison: control, interfaces and business models
3 · Mobile/cloud UI, frameworks and application architecture
4 · Government networks: acquisition, deployment and operations
5 · International standards, national law and sector rules
6 · Four parallel flows across a universal business network
9 · Six original handwritten pages — unchanged source archive
chapters.text:
Technology generations, business controllers, government procurement, international standards, four value-chain flows, and project scheduling as a unifying systems concept.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook
Every era can be analyzed through six distinct questions: (1) who builds hardware and software, (2) who owns the infrastructure, (3) who operates it, (4) who sets technical standards and legal rules, (5) who contracts and pays, and (6) who consumes the service . These roles overlap but are not equivalent. A public authority may regulate a service without owning it; a vendor may supply devices without operating the resulting network; a framework may shape an app without governing its business.
Important: this is an analytical value chain, not a universal linear hierarchy. Standards bodies, regulators, owners, suppliers and users interact in many directions.
Correction: These are overlapping historical patterns, not six clean replacements. Circuit switching remains important; mainframes still operate; REST, gRPC and AI models coexist. “API token” is usually an access credential or a metering-related concept, not the universal unit of AI billing. Model usage tokens and authentication tokens are different things.
The first page distinguishes UI medium (mobile app, SaaS web UI, dashboards, XR), framework/toolkit (Bootstrap, AngularJS, React, Next.js, Flutter, Jetpack Compose, SwiftUI, Carbon Design System), interface protocol (REST/HTTP, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket) and execution location (device, cloud, edge). These are different axes, so a mobile application can use a public open-source UI framework, a proprietary vendor SDK, a cloud-hosted backend and gRPC simultaneously.
Typical flow: user gesture → UI component → state/event handler → API client → identity/authentication → backend service → data store/stream → response/event → UI render. For live dashboards, the backend may push changes through WebSockets or server-sent events; gRPC streaming is another option depending on the client environment.
Modern attributes: responsive layouts, accessibility, reusable components, offline tolerance, multi-device behavior, measured latency, secure identity and AI assistance. “Public/private frameworks” in the notes is best interpreted as open/public ecosystems versus proprietary or organization-controlled tooling—not a standardized classification of frameworks.
Technical corrections: AngularJS is legacy and distinct from modern Angular; Bootstrap is primarily a CSS/component toolkit; Carbon is a design system, not a network protocol; Salesforce is a business platform, not simply an Android/iOS UI kit; Three.js is a 3D graphics library, while WebXR is a browser API family. Flutter, React Native, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose serve overlapping but different app-development models.
Page three sketches manufacturers → suppliers/integrators → buyers/agencies → public users . A realistic procurement process is: requirements and budget → tender/RFP and eligibility → evaluation → purchase or service agreement → design and integration → testing/acceptance → operation/maintenance → security audit and refresh. Vendor lists on the page (e.g. Cisco, Juniper, Fortinet, Dell EMC, Huawei, ZTE, Hikvision) are illustrative, not evidence of particular government contracts.
Hardware categories include routers, switches, firewalls, wireless equipment, optical transport, servers, storage and video-surveillance devices. A government agency can run its own network, outsource management, or buy connectivity from a carrier; regulatory oversight is separate from operating ownership.
Cross-link: See the earlier Atlas chapters on network devices, telecommunications infrastructure, business procurement, contracts and the difference between public and private networks. The device supply chain maps to, but is not identical with, the information-flow architecture.
The fourth page proposes a chain from global oversight to standards bodies, regional regulation, national enforcement, industry rules and market actors. The useful insight is the existence of multiple overlapping governance layers , not a single world-government chain of command.
Correction: “Global oversight → international bodies → regional regulators → national enforcement” is not a universal chain of authority. The EU is a regional legal regime, the FCC is a US national regulator, and CE marking is a conformity-marking regime rather than an agency. NHTSA, FDA, FERA and other bodies have different mandates and jurisdictions. National implementation, contracts and sector-specific obligations determine which requirements apply.
The fifth page identifies four interacting flows. This is a powerful model for comparing pre-telegraph commerce with modern platform and AI systems:
Example: a connected cold-chain shipment moves goods by road (physical), reports temperatures via IoT (information), settles invoices through banking rails (financial), and demonstrates food-safety compliance (rules). APIs, AI/ML, blockchain and IoT can support these flows, but blockchain is not a required component and AI does not replace legal accountability.
Cross-era link: a telegraph-era merchant could already coordinate these four flows using ships, letters, telegraph messages, banks and customs. Modern technology accelerates coordination and automates parts of it rather than inventing the business flows from scratch.
The sixth page uses tasks + resources → schedule and compares power generation, network bandwidth, finance and projects. A scheduler maps work onto limited resources subject to priorities, deadlines, capacity, fairness and constraints. That abstraction is useful, but each domain uses different mechanisms and governing bodies.
Correction: ISO/RTO organizations schedule parts of electric-grid operation in some jurisdictions, but are not universal electricity schedulers. BGP selects interdomain routing paths and is not a general-purpose ISP bandwidth scheduler. ICANN and regional Internet registries coordinate identifiers; they do not schedule IP packets. SWIFT is primarily a financial messaging network, not the universal entity that settles payments.
Project example: a government network rollout has tasks (survey → procure → install → configure → test → handover), resources (technicians, fiber, equipment, budget), constraints (permits, lead times, dependencies) and a schedule. This is analogous to a computer scheduler only at the abstract resource-allocation level.
History and institutions: era table links to communication/trade and standards chapters. Computer architecture and Linux: scheduling connects to the processes and runtime chapters. Network engineering: procurement, routing and QoS connect to network hardware, protocols and service operators. Cloud and applications: UI frameworks, APIs and AI usage connect to cloud and platform chapters. Business systems: four flows connect trade, finance, compliance and service contracts. AI era: distinguish AI applications carried over networks, AI-managed network operations and agent-to-agent communications.
Editorial status: this chapter is integrated into the cumulative Atlas navigation and provides explicit links between themes. It is not a claim of word-for-word transcription or complete verification of all handwritten annotations.

Technical synthesis: Repository URL is a logical path; hostname, IP, pod, and load balancer are separate identities. Local, remote, and virtual repositories have different roles.
Cross-links to prior Atlas topics: OCI registries, Helm, TLS, DNS, CI/CD, Kubernetes ingress, backup vs archive.
Technical synthesis: UART, USART, USB, GPIO, I2C, SPI, CAN, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC and MQTT are not the same abstraction. MQTT is an application protocol, GPIO a signal interface.
Cross-links to prior Atlas topics: Kernel drivers, user space, system calls, NIC, OSI, transports, IoT.
Technical synthesis: Firmware resides commonly in flash; may be updated, and initializes or controls hardware. UEFI firmware and EFI System Partition are distinct.
Cross-links to prior Atlas topics: CPU reset, bootloader, kernel, Secure Boot, storage, device drivers.
Technical synthesis: Procedural programming uses functions and parameters; OOP uses objects and encapsulation. Neither determines monolith vs microservice deployment.
Cross-links to prior Atlas topics: SOA, microservices, process models, package construction, code architecture.
Repositories on one Artifactory instance can share an endpoint, but are not inherently assigned a common IP; each repository has a distinct logical path.
Containers have internal addresses; stable service access commonly uses DNS, Service, Ingress/Gateway and/or load balancer. HA also requires correct storage/database architecture.
UART, SPI, I²C and CAN are hardware communication interfaces/buses; MQTT is a higher-level messaging protocol and GPIO is not itself a serial bus.
UEFI does not universally contain a FAT32 filesystem; the EFI System Partition is a separate FAT-formatted disk partition.
Firmware can be modified by authenticated updates; it is not universally immutable ROM.
Procedural programming supports function arguments, modules and message-passing designs; OOP is not synonymous with microservices.
Artifact repositories ↔ OCI and Helm packaging ↔ CI/CD and supply-chain integrity ↔ Kubernetes ingress, Services and DNS ↔ TLS and authentication.
Firmware ↔ CPU reset and boot chain ↔ OS kernel ↔ device drivers ↔ UART/I²C/SPI/CAN ↔ network and application transports.
Procedural/OOP ↔ modules and packages ↔ monolith/microservices/SOA; these are distinct design axes.
Artifact storage ≠ source control ≠ backup ≠ archive. Each serves a different lifecycle purpose.

Block, file and object storage are interfaces
chapters.text:
A cumulative chapter connecting CPU memory addressing to Linux block devices, virtual storage pools, containers, virtual machines and OS scheduling.
CPU addresses identify locations in a process or physical address domain. Storage devices expose blocks, which file systems can organize as files; object storage exposes a different API. Virtualization creates logical views of compute and storage resources. The operating system manages processes, memory, files, devices, access control and scheduling. Each layer has its own identifiers, permissions and failure modes.

For a byte-addressable address domain with n bits, there are 2 n distinct addresses . Thus 32 bits give 2 32 bytes = 4 GiB ; 64 bits give 2 64 bytes = 16 EiB as a mathematical upper bound, not a promise of installed or supported RAM. Modern CPUs may implement fewer virtual and physical address bits. Process virtual address space is distinct from physical RAM, and the MMU/page tables translate addresses.
A physical address identifies a location in the machine's physical address map, which can include RAM and memory-mapped I/O. It does not necessarily identify a one-byte hardware cell or a literal external CPU pin. Page frames are fixed-size units of physical memory used by paging; common 4 KiB pages are one example.
Block: addressable sectors or logical blocks exposed by a device, SAN LUN, virtual disk or cloud block volume. File: named files and directories with permissions and metadata, provided by a file system and potentially exported via NFS/SMB. Object: objects addressed through an API and key/bucket-style namespace, commonly HTTP-based (for example S3-compatible APIs). A file system is often built on block storage, but object storage is not simply another level above file storage in every implementation.
Storage virtualization presents logical storage independently of the precise underlying disks or devices. Examples include Linux LVM logical volumes, RAID, SAN virtualization, thin provisioning and distributed storage. Some solutions aggregate many devices; others virtualize a single device, or map remote resources. /dev/sda and /dev/sdb are Linux block-device names, not proof that a device is a physical HDD; names and enumeration may change. NVMe devices commonly use names such as /dev/nvme0n1 .
Physical disks / remote volumes → RAID / LVM / storage pool → logical block volume → filesystem → mount point Do not equate storage virtualization with memory virtualization: they solve different resource-abstraction problems.
Linux containers run isolated user-space processes while sharing the host Linux kernel . Namespaces provide views of resources (PID, mount, network, user and others); cgroups account for and constrain resources; capabilities, seccomp and LSM policies can reduce privileges. Image layers and overlay filesystems commonly provide a writable container filesystem view, but not every container runtime requires OverlayFS. Containers are not complete guest operating systems.
Host Linux kernel ├── Container A: processes + libraries + mount/network namespaces └── Container B: processes + libraries + mount/network namespaces Docker and Podman are container tools; Kubernetes orchestrates workloads and is not itself a kernel virtualization mechanism. OpenVZ is a different OS-level virtualization technology.
A hypervisor virtualizes hardware resources so each VM can boot a guest OS and its own kernel . KVM is a Linux kernel virtualization facility commonly used with QEMU; VMware and Oracle VirtualBox are additional examples of virtualization stacks. Guest virtual disks may be image files ( .qcow2 , .vmdk , .vdi ), block volumes or passthrough devices; the extension depends on the platform, not on the definition of a VM.
Physical server → hypervisor → VM A (guest kernel + apps) → VM B (guest kernel + apps) VM isolation is generally stronger at the kernel boundary than ordinary shared-kernel containers, but actual security depends on configuration and vulnerabilities.
Core OS functions include process/thread creation and scheduling; virtual memory and physical memory allocation; filesystem and storage management; device-driver and I/O coordination; identities, permissions and isolation; networking; interfaces such as system calls and shells; and accounting, logs and diagnostics. The CPU executes instructions ; the kernel sets policy and manages resources . CPU scheduling involves scheduler policies, run queues and dispatch/context switching, not an administrator literally handing each process a processor.
In Linux, tools such as ps , top , free , lsblk , mount , ip and journalctl let you inspect distinct layers. Performance monitoring and job scheduling may also involve separate user-space services.
All six originals are unchanged. The explanations distinguish mathematical address width from implemented hardware limits; physical from virtual addresses; block/file/object APIs from virtualization; containers from full VMs; and CPU execution from OS scheduling. This is not a verbatim transcription or a complete hardware-specific specification.

Original idea / misconception: Artifactory is only a local disk for packages.
Correct mechanism: JFrog Artifactory is a repository manager: its metadata and artifact binaries have distinct persistence concerns. Depending on edition, configuration and supported providers, binary storage may use local filesystems or remote object storage such as S3-compatible or cloud object stores. Its HTTP repository endpoints are not the same as its physical storage location. A binary provider configuration, permissions, replication, cache and backup strategy determine actual placement and durability.
Practical example: A CI pipeline publishes a 1.2 GB application image to an internal Artifactory Docker repository. Developers pull from https://artifacts.example.com, while the administrator configures supported cloud object storage as the binary backend. Developers do not need direct object-store credentials; Artifactory authenticates requests, resolves metadata and serves the artifacts.
Verification / implementation: Check the deployment’s supported binary-provider configuration and storage diagnostics; do not infer backend location from the repository URL.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: OCI registries are specifically for microservices.
Correct mechanism: An OCI registry implements distribution APIs for content-addressed manifests and blobs. Container images are common, but OCI artifacts can represent images for a monolithic service, batch jobs, tools, Helm charts or other supported artifact types. OCI packaging says how artifacts are described and transported, not whether the application uses microservices. Support for arbitrary OCI artifacts depends on registry and client.
Practical example: A single large Java monolith is packaged as one OCI image and deployed as one Kubernetes Deployment. The same registry also holds a small command-line utility image and a Helm chart artifact. None of these is required to be a microservice.
Verification / implementation: Inspect image manifests and media types with a compatible OCI client; distinguish image identity (digest) from mutable tags.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: A container automatically uses its host’s IP address.
Correct mechanism: A container normally has a network namespace, whose interfaces, routes and addresses depend on the runtime’s network mode. Docker bridge networking typically gives the container its own private address; outbound traffic may be NATed through the host and inbound access may require published ports. Host-network mode shares the host network namespace, but it is an explicit choice. Kubernetes normally gives each Pod its own routable Pod IP shared by containers in that Pod; a Service exposes a stable virtual address and Ingress/Gateway routes external HTTP traffic. Exact behavior depends on the CNI, node and cluster networking design.
Practical example: A Docker web app listens on port 8080 inside a bridge-networked container. Publishing -p 8080:8080 makes it reachable through the host address, but the container’s own IP remains different. In Kubernetes, two containers in the same Pod can communicate over localhost, while a different Pod uses the Pod IP or a Service name.
Verification / implementation: Try docker inspect and docker network inspect; compare docker run --network bridge with --network host in a safe lab. In Kubernetes inspect kubectl get pods -o wide and kubectl get svc.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: A virtual repository stores another physical copy of every artifact.
Correct mechanism: An Artifactory virtual repository is a logical aggregation endpoint over selected local and remote repositories. It provides one resolution path and can apply routing and security rules; it does not necessarily materialize a full duplicate of all artifacts. Remote repositories may cache fetched content under their configured cache policies, and local repositories hold published binaries. Repository layout, access controls and cache behavior must be considered separately.
Practical example: A Maven build uses one virtual URL that aggregates company-release, company-snapshot and a remote Maven Central proxy. The developer configures a single endpoint. Some external dependencies are fetched and cached when first requested; the virtual repository itself is not a new physical mirror of everything.
Verification / implementation: Review virtual repository membership, remote caching settings and storage usage rather than counting repository URLs as independent copies.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: UART and USART are identical, and all device communication buses behave similarly.
Correct mechanism: UART denotes asynchronous serial transmit/receive logic, commonly using TX/RX plus a shared ground and agreed baud rate. USART hardware supports synchronous as well as asynchronous modes where implemented. I²C is a shared, addressed, typically two-signal board-level bus (SDA/SCL) with pull-ups; SPI is a clocked, typically short-range peripheral interface using clock, data and chip-select lines, often with separate MOSI/MISO. CAN is a differential multi-node bus designed for robust arbitration and fault handling in electrically noisy environments. Electrical levels, transceivers, framing and software drivers matter: a UART peripheral is not automatically RS-232 compatible.
Practical example: A microcontroller reads a temperature sensor over I²C, streams debugging logs through a UART-to-USB adapter, communicates with fast flash storage using SPI, and exchanges engine-control messages over CAN through a CAN transceiver. These interfaces serve different physical and protocol needs.
Verification / implementation: Check the board schematic, controller datasheet, voltage levels, termination/pull-ups, clocking and driver configuration before wiring.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: MQTT is another wireless radio alongside Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
Correct mechanism: MQTT is an application-layer publish/subscribe messaging protocol, commonly carried over TCP/IP and often protected with TLS. Clients publish to topics through a broker; subscribers receive matching messages. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are connectivity technologies with their own radio/link stacks. MQTT may run over Wi-Fi, Ethernet, cellular or other compatible IP connectivity; it does not define a radio modulation scheme. Delivery semantics such as QoS 0/1/2 are application protocol behavior, not a guarantee that a physical wireless link never fails.
Practical example: A greenhouse sensor connects to a Wi-Fi access point, obtains an IP address, establishes a TLS connection to an MQTT broker and publishes greenhouse/temperature. A dashboard on wired Ethernet subscribes to that topic. Wi-Fi moves packets; MQTT organizes messages.
Verification / implementation: Use a packet capture or broker client to inspect MQTT CONNECT/PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE; separately inspect Wi-Fi association and IP connectivity.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: A 64-bit processor necessarily exposes 2^64 bytes of RAM.
Correct mechanism: Virtual address width, physical address width, implemented page-table modes and installed memory are distinct. A byte-addressed n-bit address space has up to 2^n addressable byte positions, but a CPU may implement fewer than 64 virtual and physical address bits. OS mappings, reserved regions and memory-management features constrain usable ranges. Physical RAM capacity depends on the platform, motherboard and memory modules.
Practical example: A 64-bit Linux server may have 32 GiB of installed RAM while supporting much larger virtual address spaces per process. Two processes can each map the same virtual address to different physical pages.
Verification / implementation: On Linux compare lscpu address sizes, free -h, /proc/meminfo and /proc/<pid>/maps; these measure different things.
Related source chapter: C27
Original idea / misconception: Block-level storage itself necessarily combines disks and organizes files.
Correct mechanism: Block storage exposes logical block devices and reads/writes addressed blocks. A filesystem layered above a block device manages directories, filenames, permissions and file metadata. Object storage exposes objects and metadata through an API, often accessed by bucket/key. Storage virtualization (LVM, RAID, SAN virtualization, software-defined storage) may aggregate, remap or provision storage, but aggregation is not a prerequisite for block access.
Practical example: An EC2-style VM attaches a block volume, formats it ext4 and mounts /data. A NAS exports a filesystem over NFS. An object bucket stores backups via S3 APIs. LVM may span multiple underlying disks, but ext4 is still responsible for the directory tree.
Verification / implementation: Compare lsblk, findmnt, lvs, df -h and an object-store client; they show different abstraction layers.
Related source chapter: C27
Original idea / misconception: Each container has its own independent operating-system kernel, or is as isolated as a VM.
Correct mechanism: A conventional VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own guest kernel; a conventional Linux container shares the host Linux kernel while isolating selected resources using namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and other security mechanisms. A container image can include user-space files and libraries without containing a running independent kernel. Containers may be nested inside VMs; stronger sandbox runtimes may use microVMs or separate kernels. Neither model is automatically secure without configuration.
Practical example: A physical host runs two KVM guests: one Linux and one Windows, each with its own kernel. Inside the Linux guest, three Docker containers run separate applications using that guest’s Linux kernel.
Verification / implementation: Compare uname -r in containers on one host, inspect namespace links in /proc, and compare guest kernel versions across VMs.
Related source chapter: C27
Original idea / misconception: Memory allocation and process scheduling are both done directly by the CPU.
Correct mechanism: The OS kernel manages virtual memory, page mappings, protection and allocation policies with hardware MMU support. CPU hardware executes instructions and translates memory accesses using the MMU/TLB. The kernel scheduler decides which runnable thread executes on a CPU; dispatch and context switching enact those decisions. Drivers, interrupt handlers and device controllers participate in I/O.
Practical example: When two applications compete for CPU, Linux scheduling policies determine runnable-thread execution. When an application calls mmap, the kernel establishes a mapping; physical pages may be populated lazily on page faults.
Verification / implementation: Inspect top/ps, /proc/<pid>/maps, vmstat and perf in an authorized lab; separate scheduler decisions from hardware execution.

Download /var/tmp/package.tar.gz — temporary transfer landing zone. Extract /var/tmp/unpack — temporary installer workspace. Install /opt/vendor/app — runtime binaries and libraries. Data mount /srv/app-data — persistent state on an appropriate filesystem or separate volume. These paths are examples, not vendor-specific defaults.
Separating data from binaries supports upgrades and backup design, but a second volume is not automatically high availability.
Generic repositories distribute arbitrary files (ZIP, tar.gz, JAR, vendor bundles). OCI registries distribute content-addressed blobs/manifests including images and some non-image artifacts. Artifact type does not determine whether software is monolithic or microservice-based. Helm charts may be published as OCI artifacts.
VM: CI → generic repository → HTTPS download → integrity check → extraction → installer → service startup.
Kubernetes: CI → OCI registry → deployment manifest/Helm → Pod scheduling → node runtime pulls image → container starts. CI need not pull the production image itself.
Distinguish host address (VM/node IP), service identity (DNS, TLS certificate, load balancer or ingress), and repository identity (logical URL path and access policy). Multiple repositories can share one Artifactory service endpoint. A remote repository may proxy an upstream artifact source; Artifactory is not inherently a general-purpose internet proxy.
Generic ≠ monolith-only; OCI ≠ microservices-only.
Repositories need not each have their own IP.
Data on another disk ≠ automatic backup, replication or HA.
OCI images and Helm charts are related but not identical artifacts.
Source code repositories and artifact repositories have different responsibilities.
Do not embed access tokens in scripts; use a protected credential store and least privilege.
Linux: shell, systemd, permissions, mounts. Storage: block volumes, SAN, snapshots, backups. Networking: DNS, TLS, routing, ingress, firewall, proxies. Containers: OCI layers, image pulls, registry credentials. Security: checksums, signatures, supply-chain provenance. Firmware: hardware initialization is a lower layer than runtime artifact delivery.
Unifying model: Source → Build → Artifact → Repository → Secure transfer → Deployment → Persistent state → Monitoring and recovery.

headings: 3 · Request–response: synchronous does not mean local or physically wired
4 · Messaging, brokers and the meaning of asynchronous
5 · Peer-to-peer: peers can still use servers
6 · Subnet address, broadcast address and VLAN ID: three different things
7 · Switches, routers, access points and virtual networks
9 · Guided, unguided and virtual media: separate the physical from logical

chapters.text:
Source handwriting preserved intact. Corrections are explained with architecture, practical scenarios, commands and connections to previous Atlas chapters.
Original: Multiple independent nodes cooperate over a network toward a common goal, overcoming limits of one physical computer.
Explanation: A distributed system is a collection of autonomous computing components coordinating by exchanging messages. Nodes may be physical servers, VMs, containers or devices. Distribution enables horizontal scaling, locality, fault tolerance and organizational separation, but adds latency, partial failure, retries, duplicate delivery, consistency and observability challenges.
Example: An online course platform runs a frontend on one service, an enrollment API on another and a database elsewhere. A request can fail halfway even though all three machines are healthy. An API timeout does not prove the database write failed; retrying blindly can create duplicate enrollments. Use an idempotency key, durable transactions and tracing.
Connection: Earlier Atlas chapters cover VM/container resource isolation; this chapter explains the protocols and architecture that connect those workloads.
Source claim: Request–response is tightly bound to standard client–server and depends on subnet ID/VLAN rather than broadcast.
Precise model: A requester sends a request and receives a corresponding response. It may be synchronous from the caller's perspective, but asynchronous APIs and nonblocking I/O can implement the same pattern. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and many gRPC methods support request–response. IP routing handles connectivity across subnets; VLANs only define Layer-2 segmentation and do not inherently determine whether request–response works.
Real example: A user in Hyderabad calls an AWS-hosted HTTPS API in Mumbai. The devices are in different networks; there is no shared VLAN or IPv4 broadcast domain. DNS resolves a hostname; the client opens a transport connection and exchanges encrypted application data.
Verify: curl -v https://example.com , ip route get 1.1.1.1 , ss -tn . A VLAN ID is not included in the end-to-end HTTP request.
Source claim: Message-driven communication needs a centralized broker, a broadcast ID and VLAN ID; subnet ID is for the broker only.
Real example: An IoT sensor on Wi-Fi publishes MQTT to a TLS-enabled broker in the cloud. A dashboard on mobile data subscribes to the topic. Neither device shares a broadcast domain with the broker. MQTT is an application-layer protocol , not a radio technology.
Asynchronous nuance: The producer need not wait for the consumer to finish work, but delivery acknowledgments, ordering, retries and durability vary by system. MQTT QoS 0/1/2 are not universal guarantees of exactly-once business processing. Kafka partitions preserve order within a partition, not across every partition.
Source claim: P2P means no central servers, exchanges subnet IDs dynamically and uses broadcast/VLAN for discovery; STUN/TURN are required.
Example: A WebRTC video call often uses a signaling server to exchange session metadata, ICE to test candidate paths, STUN to discover address mappings, and TURN when direct peer connectivity fails. It can work across distinct ISPs and VLANs. BitTorrent may use trackers and/or a distributed hash table for peer discovery.
Nuance: UDP hole punching is constrained by NAT and firewall behavior; VLAN ID is a local network label and generally not meaningful across the public Internet.
Real example: Two hosts in VLAN 20 on the same switch can communicate at L2 when correctly configured; a host in VLAN 30 usually needs L3 routing and policy to reach them. A cloud load balancer can accept HTTPS from the Internet without sharing clients' VLANs or broadcast addresses.
IPv6 distinction: IPv6 does not use broadcast; it uses multicast and other mechanisms for functions such as neighbor discovery.
Correction to the mapping: An L2 switch forwards Ethernet frames primarily by MAC address within VLANs. A router or L3 switch forwards IP packets using routing tables. A wireless AP bridges or routes wireless clients depending on its configuration. A virtual switch forwards frames between VMs/containers and uplinks; overlays such as VXLAN can extend logical segments over routed underlays.
Example: A Linux host runs two VMs on a Linux bridge; both share a VLAN-tagged uplink. A router enforces ACLs between the student VLAN and administration VLAN. Whether the applications use HTTP, MQTT or gRPC is independent of those VLAN assignments.

Correction: A “Docker network” may use bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan or other drivers; it does not automatically represent a separate physical network. Container IP behavior depends on the selected network mode.
Source: Fiber and switches were listed as guided, Wi-Fi/cellular as unguided, and Docker/VPC/vSwitch as virtual media.
Real example: A VPC packet between two cloud VMs may traverse virtual NICs, host vSwitches, an overlay tunnel, physical Ethernet switches and optical links. The logical network is distinct from the physical media underneath it.
What each layer does: HTTPS request–response submits the enrollment. A database transaction and outbox prevent lost business events. The worker consumes a queued event asynchronously. The sensor uses Wi-Fi for local radio access and MQTT for application messaging. Separate VLANs can isolate student devices from management, while firewall policies control allowed flows. The API, worker and broker may run in containers on VMs without sharing an IP subnet.
Failure analysis: If a worker crashes after sending a message but before acknowledging it, the broker may redeliver. Use idempotent processing and durable state. If the WAN fails, the sensor can buffer readings locally. If a hypervisor host fails, a cluster manager—not the hypervisor alone—may restart VMs elsewhere.

headings: Who developed, funded, owned and operated the systems?
chapters.text:
Technology, infrastructure, network architecture, institutional ownership and business economics.
Vacuum-tube electronic digital machines, stored-program memory, transistors, magnetic-core memory, magnetic tape, integrated circuits, batch monitors and time-sharing.
Universities, government laboratories, IBM, DEC, Bell Labs, semiconductor firms and defense research sponsors. These participants had different roles: research sponsorship, equipment supply, network operation, regulation, standardization and service consumption should not be conflated.
Central computer with peripherals and terminals; jobs scheduled and protected by emerging operating-system mechanisms.
Mainframe purchase or leasing, maintenance, centralized computing services, time-sharing fees.
Digital refers to discrete representation; electronic refers to implementation. The transition was from electromechanical and isolated computing to faster electronic digital, interactive and shared systems.
A payroll batch could be submitted on cards, executed by a central machine and printed later. Time-sharing subsequently let multiple terminals interact with one computer through scheduled CPU access.
Expensive computing encouraged centralized ownership; resource scheduling and access controls became economically and administratively important.

chapters.title: ⚡ From electric signals to functional silicon
headings: How a sensor reading becomes a software event
chapters.text:
Read the signal path before the chip catalog: electricity → analog conditioning → digital logic → state → conversion → computation and I/O.
Continuous-valued voltages and currents; amplifiers, oscillators, filters and sensor conditioning. Real analog systems have noise, bandwidth and nonlinearity.
Logic levels interpreted as discrete states. Combinational circuits produce outputs from current inputs; sequential circuits hold state with latches, flip-flops and registers.
ADC turns sampled analog input into digital codes; DAC reconstructs an analog output from digital codes. Clocking, reference voltage and quantization matter.
Switching regulators, MOSFET power stages and power-distribution networks convert, control and protect electrical energy.
Physical quantity → transducer → analog amplifier/filter → ADC → MCU/SoC peripheral → interrupt or DMA → driver → application → decision → DAC/PWM/actuator.
Edge meanings: transducer converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal; analog front end conditions it; ADC quantizes it; bus/peripheral exposes a register or buffer; interrupt signals completion; DMA may transfer data without CPU copying each byte; the application applies policy.
Boundary: not every design contains every stage: digital sensors may integrate an ADC and speak I²C or SPI; a purely analog feedback circuit may use no CPU.
CPU, memory, radio, PMIC, Ethernet PHY and FPGA describe functions or implementation styles . IC, package, module, PCB and SoC describe different physical integration levels. A SoC can combine CPU cores, GPU, memory controllers and peripherals, but external DRAM, storage and power components may still be required.

chapters.title: From Electrical Communication to the AI Infrastructure Economy
headings: 2. From electrical science to global signaling
3. Electronic, digital and networked computers are different dimensions
4. From dedicated machines to virtual operating environments
5. How telecommunications became public and globally interconnected
6. How a service reaches an end user anywhere in the world
7. Banking, finance, industrial production and digital business
8. The physical supply chain behind supposedly virtual services
9. Business models and operating priorities across the eras
10. The AI era through 2026: continuity and change
chapters.text:
A historical systems analysis of computing, telecommunications, financial infrastructure, enterprise architecture, public administration and global markets, from pre-telegraph communication to 2026.
Technological change is best understood as the interaction of energy, materials, information, computation, communication, institutions and commercial incentives . A semiconductor innovation changes what computers can do; a network protocol changes which computers can communicate; an operating system changes how resources are allocated; and a business model determines who can afford to deploy those capabilities at scale. The resulting system connects households, enterprises, banks, governments, carriers and cloud providers.
These layers form a network of dependencies rather than a simple chronological ladder. Older technologies coexist with newer ones.
Use the table to compare each era across technical mechanisms, network architecture, ownership, economic activity and the principal transition. The dates describe broad periods of adoption; they are not claims that all countries developed at the same pace.
Experiments with static electricity, magnetism, batteries and electromagnetism established how electric current could be generated, controlled and detected. The telegraph combined a power source, a signaling circuit, a receiver and an agreed code. Repeaters and relay stations extended practical distances; submarine cables extended communications between continents. Railway operations and financial markets benefited because information could arrive faster than physical goods.
Telephone systems added analog voice transmission and switching. Early exchanges used operators to connect circuits; later electromechanical and electronic switching reduced manual intervention. Radio added unguided transmission using electromagnetic waves, while coaxial cables, microwave links, optical fiber and satellites expanded carrying capacity and geographic reach. These media did not make earlier methods disappear: they created overlapping communication infrastructures with different cost, capacity and reliability properties.
Electronic identifies the implementation technology; digital identifies discrete information representation; networked identifies communication capability. Electronic digital computers existed by the 1940s. Early machines could be electronic and digital yet operate largely in isolation. The later transformation combined affordable semiconductor logic, operating systems, standardized interfaces and packet communication.
Modems historically mapped digital data onto signals suitable for analog telephone channels. Ethernet uses physical-layer signaling over copper or fiber; Wi-Fi and cellular systems modulate radio waves; optical systems encode information onto light. A digital message is not itself a square electrical pulse throughout the entire journey. Different media use different modulation, encoding and error-control methods.
Early computers executed jobs on scarce dedicated hardware. Batch monitors and operating systems organized workloads; multiprogramming and time-sharing shared processor time among users; memory protection and virtual memory isolated process address spaces. Mainframe virtualization later supported multiple logical machine environments. Modern hypervisors such as KVM, Hyper-V and VMware ESXi expose virtual hardware to guest operating systems, while containers isolate processes using a shared host kernel.
Virtualization does not turn an operating system into a purely imaginary system. It abstracts compute, memory, storage or networking resources while real physical machines still execute instructions and move bits. A cloud virtual network likewise relies on switches, routers, optical transport, control planes and physical facilities. Software-defined networking separates policy/control abstractions from forwarding functions; NFV moves some network appliances from dedicated boxes into software workloads.
“Public network” has multiple meanings: service offered to the public, government ownership, or traffic carried across the public Internet. These are not interchangeable. Telegraph and telephone companies sold public communication services before Internet access existed. Some countries used government-run postal, telegraph and telephone administrations; others relied more heavily on private carriers operating under regulation or franchise. Research and defense networks subsequently developed packet networking, while commercial ISPs and independent autonomous systems extended public Internet connectivity.
Standards and coordination bodies occupy different roles: ITU supports international telecommunications coordination; IETF develops Internet technical specifications through open processes; IEEE develops many networking standards; ICANN coordinates aspects of the global naming and numbering ecosystem; national regulators oversee matters within their jurisdictions. No single body owns the entire Internet.
Fixed access may use fiber-to-the-home, DSL, cable or wireless local loops; mobile access uses radio access networks and packet cores; remote regions may use satellite and other wireless backhaul. International connectivity can traverse terrestrial fiber, submarine cables, satellite links and multiple independently operated autonomous systems. A nearby CDN may answer a request without it ever crossing an ocean. DNS locates service endpoints; BGP exchanges reachability between autonomous systems; IP forwards packets; TLS secures application sessions. Connectivity is not universal: coverage, affordability, regulation, power and device availability still constrain access.
Industrial enterprises first coordinated through ledgers, postal communications and physical supply chains. Telegraph and telephone services accelerated orders, securities quotations and inter-office decisions. Punched-card processing and mainframes supported accounting, payroll, inventory and bank ledgers. Relational databases, LANs and client-server applications expanded enterprise transaction processing. MRP and MRP II evolved into integrated ERP; EDI connected business partners; the Web and APIs enabled customer-facing commerce and interoperable services.
In finance, ATM networks, card authorization, electronic funds transfer, SWIFT messaging, core banking, real-time payment systems and mobile wallets are distinct infrastructures with different governance and settlement functions. A payment instruction, a bank ledger update and final interbank settlement are not identical events. Modern commerce also depends on logistics, warehouse systems, tax and compliance systems, identity and fraud controls.
Cloud and AI depend on mines, power generation, ultrapure materials, semiconductor equipment, fabrication plants, packaging, server assembly, optical modules, data-center cooling and international logistics. Semiconductor equipment suppliers, foundries, chip designers, OEM/ODMs, telecommunications vendors, carriers and cloud operators occupy different positions in the value chain. ASML and Lam Research are examples of equipment firms; TSMC is an example of a foundry; NVIDIA designs computing hardware; network vendors and cloud providers integrate systems for end customers. This is a division of labor, not a claim that any one company alone controls the chain.
Supply-chain power arises from bottlenecks, intellectual property, standards, production yield, capital requirements, energy access, procurement and distribution. Public procurement, research grants, trade policy, competition law and spectrum licensing shape investment without making governments the technical operators of every service.
These are cumulative business options rather than mutually exclusive eras. A contemporary carrier can simultaneously sell fiber access, mobile plans, leased lines, cloud interconnects, managed security and enterprise IT services. A modern bank may retain a mainframe while operating mobile apps and cloud analytics.
AI applications add intensive model training and inference workloads to existing digital infrastructure. They increase demand for accelerators, high-bandwidth memory, fast interconnects, storage throughput, electrical power, cooling, data governance and distributed serving. They also create new operational questions: model evaluation, privacy, cybersecurity, reliability, latency, cost per inference, vendor dependence and human oversight. Agents and automation can coordinate software tools, but they do not eliminate the need for deterministic transaction systems, access controls or accountable administration.
Potential future technologies such as fault-tolerant quantum computing, brain-computer interfaces or new network architectures belong in a separate emerging research category; they should not be presented as universally deployed production infrastructure in 2026.

chapters.title: 🌐 From embedded devices to NICs, switches and cloud systems
headings: Packet journey from physical port to a service
Compare an IoT sensor, laptop and cloud server
chapters.text:
The same functional building blocks appear at different scales, but architecture changes with power, latency, reliability and throughput needs.
Trackers, wearables, sensors and headphones: MCU/SoC, on-chip RAM/flash, radios, battery management and tight energy constraints.
Phones and laptops: CPU/SoC, DRAM, flash or SSD, GPU, wireless modem, display/audio controllers and OS services.
Smart intersections, cameras and vehicles: real-time constraints, rugged interfaces, accelerators, watchdogs and security/safety engineering.
Servers and accelerators: many cores, ECC DRAM, NVMe, high-speed NICs, redundancy, orchestration and observability.
Mainframes emphasize transaction integrity, virtualization and availability; supercomputers emphasize distributed numerical throughput. They are not the same architecture.
Ethernet: application → TCP/UDP/IP stack → NIC driver → NIC MAC → Ethernet PHY → copper/fiber medium → switch/router. MAC handles link framing; PHY handles physical signaling. The NIC may also offload checksum, segmentation, virtualization or cryptographic work.
Wireless: application → network stack → Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular controller and baseband → RF transceiver/front end → antenna → air interface. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular are distinct protocol families with different link/control architectures.
Fiber: a transceiver module converts electrical signals to/from optical signals; switches and routers make forwarding decisions, not the optical module itself.
NIC receives frame → DMA to memory → interrupt or polling/NAPI → kernel driver → Ethernet/IP processing → netfilter/routing → TCP/UDP socket → user-space server → response path. A virtual machine or container adds virtual NICs, bridges, veth pairs, namespaces, overlay encapsulation or virtual switches depending on deployment.
Hardware-to-organization connection: contracts define uptime and data protection expectations; engineers select NICs, topology, software and monitoring to meet those requirements. The business and technical layers are related, but a business department is not literally a VLAN.
For each system, identify: processing core(s), memory hierarchy, persistent storage, communication MAC/PHY/radio, power regulators, clock sources, operating environment, update mechanism, security boundary and service owner. Then trace one data item end to end and annotate every conversion, protocol and trust boundary.

chapters.title: From Merchant Correspondence to AI Platforms: Technology, Infrastructure and Business by Era
headings: 2. Telegraph: information begins to outrun goods
3. Telephone, radio and public utility systems
5. Packet networks, the Internet and Web generations
6. Servers, operating systems and networks become software-managed
7. 2026: AI infrastructure builds on all previous layers
chapters.text:
A continuous account of how information speed, computing architecture, network ownership and revenue models transformed global business.
Before electrical telegraphy, merchants, bankers and governments depended on couriers, ships, postal systems, printed price lists and trusted correspondents. A transaction across distant cities required physical transport of information. Faster access to reliable commercial intelligence could confer an advantage in trading and finance. Governments controlled or licensed many routes and postal services, while private merchants and banks maintained correspondence networks.
Worked example: A merchant seeking to buy goods overseas sends a letter specifying price and quantity. The message travels with a ship; the reply may arrive weeks later. Capital is committed while prices and supply conditions can change. Faster communication reduces some information delay but does not eliminate transport, credit or counterparty risk.
Electrical signaling moved messages across wire networks far faster than physical couriers. Telegraph offices, railway lines, submarine cables, repeaters and standardized procedures formed an early communications infrastructure. Operators earned message tariffs and cable charges; financial institutions and news agencies benefited from more timely information. International agreements addressed compatibility, tariffs and administrative procedures. Public and private ownership coexisted.
Telephone exchanges enabled interactive voice communication, while radio created new broadcasting and wireless signaling systems. Manual and later automatic switches, long-distance trunk lines, broadcast transmitters, spectrum allocation and submarine cable networks required large investments. In different countries, operators ranged from state administrations to private firms with exclusive or regulated franchises. Revenue included subscriptions, metered calls, leased circuits and advertising-supported broadcasting.
Electronic digital computers used vacuum tubes and later transistors and integrated circuits to process discrete information. Batch processing, stored-program designs, magnetic storage and early operating systems enabled organizations to process payroll, inventory and financial records at scale. Time-sharing allowed multiple users to share costly computing systems. Mainframe-centered architectures linked terminals to centralized processors; the terminal was often an input/output device rather than an independent personal computer.
Terminology: “Web 0” is an informal retrospective label. Web 1.0 and 2.0 describe broad usage patterns, not formal protocol versions. “Web3” commonly refers to blockchain-based systems, whereas the Semantic Web has also been called “Web 3.0” in other contexts. Web 4.0 and Web 5.0 have no single universally adopted technical definition.
Dedicated servers evolved into shared mainframes, time-sharing, hardware virtualization, cloud VMs, containers and orchestrated services. LANs and leased WANs were complemented by VPNs, VLANs, software-defined networking and cloud virtual networks. Businesses adopted ERP, electronic payments, APIs and SaaS. A virtual machine is an isolated guest computing environment; a container is an isolated process environment sharing a kernel; a virtual network is a software-defined abstraction that still uses physical links and devices.
Modern AI systems depend on semiconductor design, manufacturing capacity, electrical power, data centers, fiber links, network routing, operating systems, container scheduling, storage, model software and distribution channels. Revenue may accrue to chip suppliers, data-center operators, cloud platforms, model providers, application developers and integrators. Governments continue to influence trade, energy, privacy, procurement, safety and competition rules.

chapters.title: From Pre-Web Networks to Web 1.0, Web 2.0 and the AI Web
headings: Before the Web: the pre-Web environment (sometimes called “Web 0.0”)
Web 1.0: documents, hyperlinks and open protocols (roughly 1990s–early 2000s)
Web 2.0: participation, platforms and programmable services (mid-2000s onward)
Web3: blockchain-based ownership and decentralized applications (2010s–2026)
chapters.text:
The World Wide Web is an application ecosystem built on the Internet, not another name for the Internet itself. Its evolution connects hypertext, networking standards, browsers, databases, open-source software, cloud infrastructure, digital markets and AI.
“Web 0.0” is an informal retrospective label, not an official W3C generation. Before the Web, networked information systems already existed: time-sharing terminals, bulletin board systems (BBS), dial-up modems, UUCP, electronic mail, FTP, Telnet, Usenet, Gopher and proprietary services. ARPANET, research networks and enterprise WANs were not Web sites. Users could communicate and retrieve files, but there was no single universal browser-and-hyperlink model.
Protocols, addressing, access rights and pricing depended on the network and service provider.
Tim Berners-Lee's work at CERN led to the Web's foundational combination of URLs/URIs, HTTP and HTML . Early Web publishing centered on documents served by HTTP servers and rendered in browsers. Static HTML was common, but CGI scripts, server-side programming, cookies and databases also existed: Web 1.0 was not exclusively static .
Stack: client browser → DNS resolution → TCP connection → HTTP request → web server → HTML and linked assets. Popular implementations included NCSA HTTPd, Apache HTTP Server, Netscape Navigator, early Internet Explorer, Perl CGI, PHP, Java and relational databases. Open standards enabled different vendors' systems to interoperate.
Participants: CERN and W3C; university researchers; NCSA; browser vendors; ISPs; hosting providers; web publishers; online retailers and public institutions. Economics: dial-up access, hosting, web development, subscriptions, online catalogs and early banner advertising.
“Web 2.0” describes a change in dominant application and business patterns, not a new Internet protocol. Users increasingly authored content, interacted in real time and participated in social networks, marketplaces and collaborative platforms. AJAX, JavaScript engines, XML/JSON, REST-style APIs, RSS/Atom, server-side frameworks and content-management systems supported rich applications.
Stack: browser/mobile app → CDN and API gateway → web application → identity and authorization → database, search, cache and message broker. Infrastructure evolved from dedicated servers toward virtual machines, cloud services, containers and managed databases.
Participants: Wikipedia contributors, Mozilla, Apache communities, Linux developers, Google, Facebook, YouTube, WordPress, GitHub, Amazon, Salesforce, telecom carriers and cloud operators. Economics: user-generated content, targeted advertising, transaction commissions, SaaS subscriptions, freemium plans and developer ecosystems. Platform effects increased the value of participation while creating new concentration and moderation challenges.
Web3 commonly refers to blockchain-based wallets, smart contracts, tokenized assets, decentralized finance and decentralized applications. It is distinct from the older Semantic Web / “Web 3.0” vision associated with machine-readable linked data and ontologies. Neither usage represents a universal replacement of Web 2.0.
Technologies: cryptographic signatures, public-key wallets, distributed ledgers, consensus mechanisms, Ethereum-compatible smart contracts, decentralized storage systems such as IPFS, and browser-based applications that often still rely on conventional hosting and APIs. Participants: open-source protocol contributors, Ethereum ecosystem developers, standards groups, infrastructure providers, exchanges, financial institutions and regulators. Business models: network transaction fees, application services, custody, protocol infrastructure and token-related activities, with material regulatory and security risks.
Foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation, vector search, multimodal interfaces and agent workflows add new ways to discover, create and act on information. AI agents can call APIs and tools, but the underlying Web still relies on DNS, HTTP(S), identity, databases, software supply chains, cloud and physical networks. “Web 4.0” and “Web 5.0” are speculative and inconsistently defined marketing/research labels , not ratified technical generations.
Current stack: user or agent → browser/app → identity → API gateway → orchestration → search/vector retrieval → model inference → business systems → audit and governance. AI does not remove the need for trusted data, software verification, permissions or human oversight.
A 1990s training center might publish an HTML brochure and receive enquiries by email. A Web 2.0 platform adds forms, accounts, payments, reviews, scheduling and a CRM. A modern platform may add APIs, mobile notifications, online assessments, AI tutoring and automated operations. Each new layer changes identity management, database design, security, hosting costs and revenue models; it does not make the earlier network protocols disappear.

chapters.title: Global Digital Delivery: Networks, Operators, Platforms and Revenue
headings: From a household device to an overseas service
Historical transformation of network and business architecture
Case study: enterprise SD-WAN and cloud
chapters.text:
An Internet service reaches a person through a chain of independently operated systems: device manufacturers, access networks, transit and peering, DNS, cloud and content infrastructure, application software, identity, payment systems and regulators. Every layer has its own architecture, commercial contracts and failure modes.
Actual routes vary; an edge cache can satisfy a request without reaching a distant origin. Fiber, copper, terrestrial radio and satellite links carry the physical signals.
Dedicated circuits and terminals: fixed leased links and centralized mainframes, with hardware-heavy capital expenditure and per-line or equipment contracts. Client-server and enterprise WAN: branch LANs, databases, routers, leased circuits and VPNs; enterprises manage identity and application access. Web and e-commerce: browser access over ISPs and Internet backbones; hosting and online payments extend reach beyond branches. Cloud-native: virtual networks, load balancers, APIs, containers, CDNs and managed data; businesses buy metered capacity and managed services. AI-intensive: specialized accelerators, model APIs, data governance and observability add new costs and capabilities to existing digital platforms.
A customer accesses a store from a mobile device. The access carrier connects the device to the Internet; DNS identifies service endpoints; TLS protects application transport; a CDN may serve assets; an application checks inventory in a database; a payment provider coordinates authorization; logistics providers fulfill the order. Government authorities influence consumer protection, tax, privacy, spectrum and payment rules. A merchant may pay cloud usage, payment processing, connectivity, software subscriptions and advertising fees to different organizations.
A business with multiple branches can combine broadband and private links using SD-WAN policies and encrypted overlays. Traffic may flow to a data center, SaaS platform or cloud virtual private network. Underlay networks remain physically owned and operated by carriers; overlay routing and segmentation are software-controlled. SD-WAN is not the same as replacing the Internet or creating a new physical medium.
Linux, OpenSSH, HTTP servers, DNS implementations, databases, Kubernetes and observability libraries often support these services. Commercial software, proprietary network equipment, regulated payment rails and public infrastructure remain equally significant.
