From a sensor to a cloud dashboard
From an NVMe file to a CPU instruction
Eight distinctions that prevent conceptual confusion
chapters.text:
This chapter reads the latest 15 pages individually rather than treating them as a single topic. Each entry separates source topics from editorial elaboration/correction . Earlier source pages remain preserved in the source gallery, but are not falsely marked as individually audited.
Source observation = a careful topical reading of the photographed page, not a certified verbatim transcription. Technical expansion = independently written explanation and correction. Cross-links = related chapters. Where handwriting is faint or ambiguous, use the original photograph as authoritative.
Communication/interface chips: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modems, display drivers; programmable logic: FPGA.
A wireless modem integrates baseband/control functions, but radio front-end, antenna and host interface may be separate. Display drivers convert pixel/control data into electrical drive signals. FPGA is reconfigurable digital hardware rather than a generic blank chip.
Related chapters: C09 · C11
Analog amplifiers, filters, oscillators; digital logic gates, combinational and sequential circuits; mixed-signal ADC/DAC; power circuits.
Analog signals are continuous in amplitude, while digital circuits interpret voltage ranges as logic states. Combinational logic depends on present inputs; sequential logic depends on state and clock/event history. ADCs sample and quantize; DACs reconstruct analog levels. Power circuits convert/regulate energy, not merely heavy current.
Related chapters: C08 · C10
Logic/processing CPU GPU MCU ASIC; memory DRAM SRAM NAND EEPROM; PMIC voltage and battery management; RF/Ethernet/display/audio; linear and timer chips.
Classify by function, not packaging: CPU and GPU may share a SoC; an MCU includes CPU and peripherals; ASIC describes custom-purpose implementation. DRAM is volatile, NAND is persistent, EEPROM supports small rewritable nonvolatile storage. PMIC includes rails, sequencing and protection.
Related chapters: C08 · C09 · C10
Micro standalone trackers/headphones: MCU, SRAM, firmware storage, Bluetooth RF, battery chips. Personal devices: CPU/SoC, DRAM, NAND, modem, display driver, audio codec.
A tracker can be an SoC with embedded flash and radio rather than multiple separate ICs. ARM is an ISA family, not itself a microcontroller. Smartphone SoCs combine application CPU, GPU, NPU and peripherals, often with separate RF/power components.
Related chapters: C09 · C10 · C11
Edge: traffic lights, autonomous vehicles, FPGAs, NPUs, ECC RAM and rugged PMICs. Data center: server blades, CPUs/GPUs, DDR5, NVMe and smart NICs.
Safety-critical edge controllers require deterministic behavior, watchdogs and fail-safe design; an FPGA is not required for every edge system. ECC detects/corrects certain memory errors. SmartNIC/DPU offloads networking/storage/security tasks but does not replace the host CPU.
Related chapters: C10 · C11
IBM Z mainframes, HBM, interconnect switching, distributed clusters and supercomputers.
Mainframes emphasize resilient transaction processing, I/O, partitioning and availability; HPC systems emphasize parallel numerical throughput. HBM is used in many accelerators but is not the defining memory for all mainframes. Cluster interconnects differ from ordinary Ethernet depending on design.
Related chapters: C09 · C10 · C11
CPU runs OS/applications; GPU accelerates graphics/AI; MCU firmware; NPU neural workloads; ASIC fixed logic; FPGA reconfigurable. SRAM/DRAM/ROM/flash/GDDR/HBM. PCIe USB Ethernet SATA NVMe I²C SPI Wi-Fi BLE RF front-end NFC GPS.
PCIe/USB/I²C/SPI are buses/interconnects, Ethernet and Wi-Fi are network families, NVMe is a storage command protocol, and SATA is a storage interface. NFC and GNSS/GPS have distinct communication/positioning roles. An FPGA configuration is hardware logic, not just editable software.
Related chapters: C09 · C10 · C11
CPUs GPUs MCUs NPUs FPGAs ASICs; single-chip SoC, motherboard integration, chip functions for personal/cloud/distributed computing.
SoC refers to integration of multiple functional blocks on one die, not necessarily all device components. A motherboard contains packages, buses and connectors; a module may contain several chips. CISC/RISC and ASIC/FPGA are independent classification axes.
Related chapters: C09 · C10
SRAM cache L1/L2/L3; DRAM DDR4/DDR5 LPDDR; HBM 3D stacks; NAND SSDs; EEPROM/NOR firmware; bus communication and DMA.
SRAM commonly implements cache but cache is a managed hierarchy, not just a chip. DRAM requires refresh. HBM stacks memory dies with high bandwidth. NAND is erased in blocks and programmed in pages; SSD controller manages wear-leveling and flash translation. EEPROM and NOR differ in access/erase granularity. DMA transfers data without CPU copying every byte, but CPU/software still configures it.
Related chapters: C10 · C11
PMIC/VRM power conversion; embedded controller; cache controller; integrated memory controller; NVMe/USB storage controllers; ports and buses.
A VRM supplies regulated voltage; PMIC may sequence rails and handle charging. Cache controllers track tags/coherence; memory controllers schedule DRAM commands; SSD controllers manage NAND. A USB port is a connector/transport endpoint, not inherently master/slave. Ethernet is switched packet networking, not merely peer-to-peer.
Related chapters: C08 · C10 · C11
CPU GPU MCU NPU SoC ASIC DSP FPGA; processing as brain, memory as storage, communications as messenger, PMIC as fuel system, timer as synchronization.
Analogy is pedagogical, not literal: devices can operate autonomously and use DMA/interrupts. A GPU is itself a processor; a SoC is a package of subsystems; DSP targets signal operations; an ASIC may contain a CPU. Clocks synchronize circuitry while OS schedulers decide which software task runs.
Related chapters: C09 · C10
Processing executes software; memory holds active/persistent data; power distributes regulated rails; communication interfaces connect systems; linear/timer handles analog and clock signals.
Not every digital device uses five physically separate chips; integrated SoCs collapse several families, while some analog devices need no programmable processor. ROM and NAND differ; RF transceivers, MACs and PHYs occupy different protocol layers.
Related chapters: C08 · C09 · C10
RISC/CISC, ARM/x86-64, application-specific ASIC, reconfigurable FPGA, MCU for simpler devices; general-purpose CPU/SoC for complex devices.
ISA (ARM, x86, RISC-V) differs from microarchitecture and implementation substrate (ASIC/FPGA). RISC does not guarantee low power and CISC does not guarantee performance. ASIC fixed-function hardware can include programmable embedded cores; FPGA logic can implement CPUs.
Related chapters: C09
Battery-focused RISC, high-performance CISC, ASIC networking/embedded, FPGA telecom/aerospace/hardware development.
These are tendencies, not strict mappings: Arm servers are high performance; x86 laptops can be power efficient; ASICs are used widely for high-volume acceleration; FPGAs can be production deployed in networks. Compare workloads, software ecosystem, latency, power and unit economics.
Related chapters: C09 · C11
Wireless RF front-end, USB device/tracking, satellite modem; wired optical transceiver, PCIe switch, Thunderbolt controller; network chip ASIC, PHY, flash, NIC, VLAN.
RF front-end conditions radio signals; baseband/modem processes protocol waveforms. Optical transceiver converts electrical/optical signals; a PCIe switch routes PCIe transactions; a network switch ASIC forwards Ethernet frames. PHY handles physical-layer signaling; NIC joins host memory/driver to a link. VLAN is a logical segmentation mechanism implemented in switch/NIC software/hardware, not a separate chip.
Related chapters: C10 · C11

Every edge has a different responsibility: conversion, conditioning, sampling, device access, buffering, framing, modulation, packet forwarding, kernel delivery, transport security and application processing. chapters.title: How Shared Technology Became Proprietary Ecosystems
headings: Open foundations do not imply open commercial control
chapters.text:
Open protocols, public research, contributor communities, cloud platforms and the economics of integration.
Companies can build proprietary products on open protocols and software while contributing improvements upstream. A company may control customer identity, billing, service-level commitments, cloud infrastructure, application distribution or proprietary extensions even when Linux, HTTP, PostgreSQL or Kubernetes support the product. The economic moat is often integration, reliability, scale, distribution and data—not sole ownership of the underlying code.
The Web was conceived at CERN in 1989, and its core software was released to the public domain in 1993. This made interoperable hypertext and client/server publishing easier to adopt. Commercial opportunities then emerged in hosting, browsers, search, online payments, advertising and application platforms. The public release of software did not grant any one company ownership of the Web.
Android uses a Linux-based software stack with a hardware abstraction layer, runtime and application framework. Device manufacturers and application developers build products on these foundations, while platform operators can retain control over proprietary service packages, compatibility requirements, distribution arrangements and customer relationships.
Kubernetes began at Google and was contributed to the CNCF in 2015. Google, Red Hat and many others have participated in its development. Cloud providers now sell managed clusters, identity integrations, networking, storage, security and monitoring. This illustrates “collaborate on common infrastructure, compete on services,” although ecosystem dependencies and proprietary integrations still matter.
Amazon built substantial operational computing capabilities for online retail. AWS launched S3 and EC2 in 2006, providing programmable storage and compute to external customers. Open-source components, standardized Internet connectivity, virtualization, data centers and proprietary engineering together enabled a new usage-based business. This is a transformation from internal IT capability to a commercial infrastructure platform—not evidence that AWS was simply a government network converted to private ownership.
Open-source contributors include volunteers, paid employees, research institutions, foundations and independent maintainers. Commercial use creates security and maintenance obligations: licensing compliance, software bills of materials, vulnerability response, provenance and dependency governance. “Free to obtain” is not the same as “free to operate.”

chapters.title: Industrial Evolution: From Merchant Networks to AI Ecosystems
headings: How industries and their networks evolve
Four transitions that changed nearly every industry
Participants: who is the customer, vendor, partner or operator?
Documented ecosystems versus illustrative industry chains
How an industry network reaches a customer anywhere
Regional comparison: India, United States, EU and China
Selected primary institutional and technical references
chapters.text:
Industries, supply chains, business relationships, market power, technical infrastructure and end-user demand from pre-telegraph trade to 2026.
Industrial history cannot be reduced to computing generations. Markets are systems of production, logistics, communications, financing, governance and consumption. A change in one layer—such as the telegraph, electrification, a programmable controller, a standardized shipping container, a database, the Internet or machine learning—changes coordination costs and often reorganizes the firms that participate.
Prices, orders, credit instructions and shipping documents traveled by messenger, post, courier or vessel. Merchant houses depended on agents, correspondents and trusted brokers. Governments built roads, administered postal services, chartered enterprises and collected customs duties. For example, East India Company trade involved ships, warehouses, chartered privileges, regional producers and financial intermediaries. Such arrangements should not be confused with today's open, competitive global markets: political power and exclusive trading rights shaped access.
Telegraph messages separated the movement of information from the movement of goods. Rail dispatch, commodity quotations, shipping instructions and financial communication could be coordinated more quickly. Telephone networks later enabled real-time conversations, while electric power and industrial machinery changed production. The effects were uneven: access depended on infrastructure, price, geography and political control.
Electronic digital computers existed by the 1940s; they did not emerge only after an allegedly separate electronic-computer era. Transistors and integrated circuits increased reliability and lowered cost over time. Businesses adopted batch accounting, mainframe reservation systems, MRP, ERP, EDI, databases, barcodes, ATMs, digital exchanges, electronic payments and enterprise networking. Digitization meant encoding information in machine-processable form; virtualization later enabled shared computing and network resources without eliminating physical infrastructure.
Commercial Internet connectivity, the Web, APIs, cloud platforms and mobile devices linked suppliers, workers and consumers. Open-source components lowered entry barriers, while proprietary platforms created new forms of distribution control. Machine learning and generative AI are increasingly applied to forecasting, document processing, fraud detection, industrial operations and customer service, subject to reliability, safety, privacy and sector-specific requirements.
B2C: an enterprise sells directly to a household or individual, such as a telecom subscription or retail purchase. B2B: a business supplies another business, such as an industrial automation vendor or cloud provider. B2G/G2B: procurement, licenses, taxes and public-service contracts connect firms and administrations. B2B2C: a technology or payment provider supports a merchant that serves the end consumer. Marketplace/platform: an operator coordinates multiple participant groups. Cooperatives and public utilities: participants or public bodies may own or govern essential shared services. One company can occupy multiple roles simultaneously.
Participants: Farmers; traders; processors; distributors; grocers; households. Real-world examples: John Deere equipment; Cargill trading and processing; Walmart retail; India’s e-NAM agricultural marketplace.
The value network includes upstream material or service providers, operating organizations, distribution partners, finance, end customers and public oversight. The specific contract and degree of integration vary by jurisdiction and period.
Participants: Depositors; borrowers; merchants; banks; clearing institutions; investors; regulators. Real-world examples: JPMorgan Chase banking; Visa and Mastercard card networks; SWIFT messaging; NPCI UPI infrastructure.
Participants: Suppliers; OEMs; contract manufacturers; dealers; industrial buyers. Real-world examples: Siemens industrial automation; Toyota production systems; SAP enterprise software.
Participants: Shippers; carriers; freight forwarders; ports; warehouses; receivers. Real-world examples: Maersk shipping; DHL logistics; FedEx express networks; Amazon fulfillment.
Participants: Spectrum authorities; tower companies; carriers; ISPs; enterprises; subscribers. Real-world examples: AT&T, BT, Deutsche Telekom, China Mobile, Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio, BSNL.
Participants: Designers; foundries; equipment makers; OEMs; developers; enterprises. Real-world examples: Arm licensing; NVIDIA design; TSMC foundry; ASML lithography; Intel integrated manufacturing.
Participants: Generators; grid operators; distributors; industrial users; households. Real-world examples: GE Vernova grid equipment; Schneider Electric controls; NTPC generation; Power Grid Corporation of India transmission.
Participants: Brands; wholesalers; marketplaces; merchants; payment providers; shoppers. Real-world examples: Walmart stores; Amazon marketplace; Shopify merchant software; Flipkart e-commerce.
Participants: Patients; providers; insurers; labs; pharmaceutical firms; public health agencies. Real-world examples: Siemens Healthineers imaging; Pfizer pharmaceuticals; Apollo Hospitals care delivery.
Participants: Creators; publishers; advertisers; distributors; platforms; audiences. Real-world examples: BBC broadcasting; Disney content; Netflix streaming; YouTube creator platform.
Participants: Citizens; agencies; contractors; institutions; teachers; students. Real-world examples: NSF-funded research networks; India Stack components; Aadhaar/UIDAI; universities and NRENs.
Participants: Owners; developers; contractors; architects; lenders; tenants. Real-world examples: Autodesk design software; Siemens building systems; CBRE property services.
Participants: Governments; prime contractors; suppliers; research laboratories; civilian users. Real-world examples: NASA public research; ISRO space programs; Airbus aircraft; SpaceX launch services.
Open-source-to-cloud: Linux, PostgreSQL, Apache, Kubernetes and related software are developed through communities, companies and foundations. Cloud providers package such components into managed services, add operational tooling and charge for capacity, convenience and service commitments. Use of open source does not imply that all platform features are open or that all contributors have equal control.
India's payments ecosystem: banks, NPCI, payment-service providers, merchants and consumers occupy different roles. UPI is a shared payment interface and scheme; individual payment applications are distribution and user-experience layers. Payment authorization, clearing, settlement and banking supervision must be distinguished.
Semiconductor ecosystem: Arm licenses processor intellectual property; fabless firms such as NVIDIA design chips; foundries such as TSMC manufacture chips for customers; equipment companies such as ASML supply production machinery. This is an illustrative value-chain description, not a claim that every named firm contracts with every other named firm.
Retail and fulfillment: Amazon combines marketplace intermediation, first-party retail, fulfillment, advertising and AWS cloud infrastructure. Walmart operates stores, e-commerce and logistics. These are examples of overlapping horizontal expansion, vertical integration and platform economics—not proof of monopoly in every market.
Industry growth can be driven by lower transaction costs, network effects, scale economies, improved infrastructure, regulation or changing demand. Decline can follow technological substitution, debt, commoditization, poor execution or regulatory change. Historical examples include the reduction of standalone telegraph services as telephony and digital messaging expanded; the decline of many proprietary minicomputer business models with PCs and commodity servers; and the shift from packaged software toward subscriptions and cloud services. Older systems often persist where migration is expensive or reliability requirements are stringent.
Market categories: natural monopoly describes cost structures that can favor one network operator; legal monopoly derives from exclusive rights; oligopoly denotes a few major competitors; competitive markets have more independent sellers; and a platform may create gatekeeping power even when its underlying communications standards are open. Government ownership, private ownership and public accessibility are separate dimensions. Antitrust, sector regulation, interoperability rules and procurement policy can constrain market power without requiring government ownership.
A smartphone communicates through a mobile radio access network or Wi-Fi and fixed broadband, reaches an Internet service provider and interconnected networks, and contacts an application often hosted on a cloud or CDN. A merchant's payment service communicates with banks and payment networks. Warehouse systems and carriers move goods physically. Trade policy, consumer law, data protection, customs and financial rules govern different stages. The end user may be an individual, a business purchaser, a public institution or a machine acting under delegated authority.
These are high-level comparisons. Market shares, current ownership, bilateral trade rules and legal obligations require date-specific verification before formal publication.
Likely pressures include greater demand for electricity and cooling from AI infrastructure, industrial automation, advanced chip packaging, sovereign-cloud requirements, cybersecurity, data-localization rules, satellite connectivity and platform interoperability. None implies that all industries will converge on one architecture. Mature sectors often combine decades-old physical infrastructure with modern APIs and AI applications.
Examples illustrate documented organizational roles or established technologies; this study does not assert specific bilateral partnerships without corresponding primary-source evidence. Detailed company histories and dated market data remain subjects for future verification.

An annotated continuation of B011: from ISP optical termination and campus network topology to Linux routing, packet filtering, network namespaces, virtual NICs and infrastructure abstractions.
Source integrity: each handwritten scan is embedded unchanged below. Technical interpretations and corrections are separately labeled. This is a careful topic-level reading, not a certified word-for-word transcription.
From the page: loopback; physical wired Ethernet; wireless interface; network bridge; virtual Ethernet; tunnel/VPN; device identity (MAC, serial); network identity (IP, VLAN, SSID, routing). The illustrated path is ISP backbone → ISP-side OLT → modem/ONT → edge router → firewall cluster → core switches → distribution switch → access switches → Wi-Fi APs / NICs / industrial gateway → IDS/IPS/HSM → ADC .
Clarifications: an OLT is the provider-side termination in a passive optical network; an ONT/ONU is typically the customer-side fiber termination, often integrated with a home gateway. “Modem” is a generic label and does not describe every fiber termination accurately. A firewall cluster is one deployment choice, not a mandatory stage. IDS/IPS and HSM are not normally chained as equivalent inline hops: IDS may monitor mirrored traffic, IPS can be inline, and HSM supplies cryptographic key operations. ADC/load balancing is commonly deployed in front of selected applications, not universally after every endpoint.
Identity layers: MAC addresses identify interfaces within a link-layer domain (and may be virtualized); IP addresses are Layer-3 locators; VLAN tags partition Layer-2 broadcast domains; SSIDs identify wireless networks; routes determine forwarding next hops. Serial numbers are inventory identifiers, not packet forwarding addresses.
From the page: edge router → iptables/nftables and ip route ; eth0 / eth1 as WAN/LAN interfaces; firewall → Netfilter and iptables/firewalld/nftables; switches → Linux bridge and ip link ; NIC/HBA → TUN/TAP and veth pairs; load balancers → HAProxy and NGINX.
Correction: ip route manipulates kernel routing tables. iptables and nft configure packet-filtering/NAT rules via kernel facilities; they are not themselves routing tables. firewalld is a management layer over firewall backends. eth0 and eth1 are interface names, not intrinsically WAN or LAN. Current Linux often uses predictable names such as enp3s0 .
Bridges: Linux bridge forwards Layer-2 frames among attached ports; ip link manages interface state and link configuration, while the bridge utilities or bridge command manage bridge forwarding details. A veth pair behaves like two connected virtual Ethernet ports and is common between a container namespace and host bridge. TUN exposes Layer-3 packets; TAP exposes Layer-2 frames. VPN is a use case for TUN, not a synonym for it.
Useful commands: ip -br link , ip -br addr , ip route show , ip rule show , bridge link , bridge vlan show , sudo nft list ruleset , ip netns list , ss -tulpn . Some commands require privileges and installed tooling.
From the page: physical devices include routers, switches, firewalls, access points, modems, NICs, load balancers, IDS/IPS, repeaters and encoders. Physical media include CAT Ethernet cable, fiber/DSL, RF spectrum, PCIe, and transceivers. Virtual equivalents include VLANs, VPN tunnels, VXLAN, GRE, virtual NICs, VIPs, iSCSI and FCoE.
Key distinction: a physical port is a hardware connector/interface; a virtual interface is a software-managed networking endpoint. A physical cable is a transmission medium, whereas a virtual link is a logical connectivity relationship implemented over underlying physical media. A packet or frame is a protocol data unit, not a direct virtual replacement for an analog/electrical/optical signal. A physical network can host multiple logical networks using VLAN, VRF and overlay encapsulation.
Multiplexing: a single Ethernet trunk can carry multiple VLANs; an IP underlay can carry multiple VXLAN VNIs; a physical NIC can expose multiple virtual functions using SR-IOV. None of these removes dependence on the physical bandwidth, optics, switches and failure domains beneath.
Original second mapping: device→virtual resource, port→interface, cable→link, path→route, plug→attachment, signal→packet/frame, physical network→logical network. These are design analogies , not one-to-one replacements.

A TCP connection ends at a proxy if the proxy terminates it and creates a separate upstream connection.

Interpretation: a service runs under an identity, while kernel mechanisms mediate resource access. An account is not a process; a daemon is a process, often with a dedicated service identity.
alice:x:1001:1001:Alice:/home/alice:/bin/bash username:hash:lastchg:min:max:warn:inactive:expire:reserved /etc/passwd: username, password placeholder, UID, primary GID, GECOS, home, login shell. /etc/shadow: nine fields: username, password hash or lock marker, password-aging and expiration fields. Hashing is not reversible encryption. NSS may retrieve network accounts through LDAP/SSSD, not just /etc/passwd.
id alice getent passwd alice sudo getent shadow alice ps -eo pid,user,group,comm Correction: system UID ranges are distribution-configurable, not universally 1–999; a service identity may have no interactive login shell; UID 0 is privileged root identity, not necessarily only an account named root.
The same library or artifact may be at rest in Artifactory, in transit over HTTPS, and in use when mapped into memory. Encryption at rest, encryption in transit and runtime isolation solve different threats.
Correction: Kubernetes volumes are mounts backed by diverse volume sources, not necessarily empty directories. A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage; it is not automatically a backup or high-availability guarantee.
A shell parses and executes commands; it does not directly convert commands to machine code. Programs use syscalls (often via libraries). Linux containers share the host kernel; VMs have separate guest kernels. Namespaces isolate views (PID, network, mount, IPC, user); cgroups track and limit resources.
Vendor base image and supported extension paths depend on the exact IBM Sterling edition and release. Pin digest, validate signatures and licensing, scan dependencies, preserve the supported runtime UID, and do not place secrets inside images. Helm renders/manages Kubernetes release manifests; controllers reconcile workloads and node runtimes pull images.
kubectl create secret docker-registry ibm-registry \ --docker-server=registry.example.com \ --docker-username='<service-account>' \ --docker-password='<access-token>' \ --namespace=sterling Security: illustrative only; avoid credentials in shell history and use managed secret injection. imagePullSecrets are for image pulls, not necessarily application database authentication. headings: 3. Why industries grow, consolidate or decline
chapters.text:
A comparative framework for monopoly, oligopoly, vertical and horizontal integration, and the changing balance of public and private authority.
Growth: a new technology reduces costs or creates demand. For example, fiber optics and packet switching helped expand long-distance digital communication capacity. Consolidation: high fixed costs, acquisitions, economies of scale and network effects can reduce the number of major operators. Decline: a legacy product loses demand when a substitute is cheaper or more capable, such as dedicated consumer dial-up access being displaced by broadband. Reconfiguration: an old technology persists in a different niche; mainframes remain important in some transaction-processing environments.
Control can shift at one layer without shifting everywhere. In the Internet era, state-funded research networking expanded into privately operated access and backbone services; governments retained spectrum administration, rights-of-way, competition law, procurement and security powers. In the cloud era, companies gained extensive control over virtual compute, identity, deployment and application marketplaces; regulators responded with privacy, competition and sector-specific requirements.
A government can allocate spectrum while a private operator builds radio towers; a standards organization can specify a protocol while a cloud provider controls its implementation and billing; a bank can own a customer relationship while depending on shared payment infrastructure; an open-source project can publish source code while trademarks and hosted services remain independently controlled. To analyze power rigorously, distinguish ownership, operation, standard-setting, access policy, pricing, regulation and data governance .
References support the institutional background and technical definitions. Interpretive comparisons and illustrative models are identified as analysis rather than established causal findings.

headings: B015 · Page 1: Memory hierarchy and Linux allocation
B015 · Page 2: RAM, page allocator, page structs and tmpfs
B015 · Page 3: Volatile RAM versus nonvolatile storage
B015 · Page 4: Backup and recovery paths
B015 · Page 6: UMA, NUMA, shared and distributed memory

Applied path: a web request and memory
chapters.text:
This chapter deepens earlier chapters on hardware, Linux processes, containers, storage and distributed systems. Original notes are shown unaltered; editorial corrections are separate.
Reading path: CPU request → virtual address → page tables / TLB → physical frame → NUMA locality → storage and recoverability.
Editorial technical synthesis: Pages, process segments, NUMA nodes and physical memory zones describe different concerns. Pages are fixed-size virtual-memory units; frames are physical RAM units. Segments are logical regions such as text, data, heap and stack. NUMA nodes group memory by locality, while zones express allocation constraints. These are not four levels of one hierarchy.
Source: B015/P01 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Editorial technical synthesis: DRAM stores volatile bytes. Linux tracks physical page frames through struct page metadata (with newer folio abstractions), and allocates them using page allocators such as the buddy allocator. tmpfs is a memory-backed filesystem with possible swap backing, not a general-purpose page allocator. The page cache accelerates file I/O.
Source: B015/P02 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Editorial technical synthesis: RAM holds active working data; NAND flash and NVMe SSDs retain data without power. NVMe is a storage interface/protocol, not a memory technology. Data can be copied between storage and RAM, but a backup must be an independently recoverable copy, not merely a live RAM workspace.
Source: B015/P03 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Editorial technical synthesis: Backups protect recoverable data and configuration. Tools mentioned include rsync, tar, dd, gzip and zstd; each has a different role. rsync copies/synchronizes files, tar archives, compression tools reduce size, and dd copies raw blocks. Redis persistence and tmpfs are not interchangeable with durable backup systems. Verify restoration, retention and off-site copies.
Source: B015/P04 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Editorial technical synthesis: Linear addressing, segmentation, paging and segmentation-plus-paging are address translation and organization mechanisms. Modern x86-64 Linux primarily uses paging with a largely flat segmentation model. Virtual addresses are translated via page tables and hardware translation caches (TLBs).
Source: B015/P05 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Editorial technical synthesis: UMA and NUMA describe memory access latency characteristics within shared-memory multiprocessor machines. NUMA memory is shared-address-space but local versus remote accesses may differ in latency. Distributed-memory nodes have separate address spaces and communicate explicitly, usually over a network. SMP and MPP are architecture labels, not mutually exclusive synonyms for UMA and distributed memory.
Source: B015/P06 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Editorial technical synthesis: ISA names such as x86-64, ARM and RISC-V are distinct from memory architecture. Cache-coherence and memory locality affect multicore performance. SIMD and vector units describe instruction/data parallelism; MIMD describes multiple independent instruction streams. NUMA-aware placement can improve performance when workloads and memory remain local.
Source: B015/P07 · original image preserved · interpretations and corrections editorial.
Earlier hardware and chip chapters: DRAM cells, controllers, PCIe and NVMe explain the hardware behind page frames and persistent storage. Linux process chapter: text, data, BSS, heap and stack are virtual-memory mappings of a process. Containers: cgroups account/limit memory; namespaces isolate views but do not create private physical RAM. Kubernetes: scheduler requests and limits are resource policies; Linux enforces memory accounting and OOM behavior on nodes. Networks and distributed systems: a remote NUMA node is not the same as remote RAM across a network; distributed memory requires explicit communication or specialized software.
NIC receives packet → kernel networking allocates buffers → application process accesses virtual addresses → CPU MMU translates addresses to physical frames → caches and NUMA locality affect latency → database or filesystem writes eventually persist to storage → separate backups enable recovery. These steps are a conceptual path, not a guarantee that every packet follows precisely the same allocation sequence.

chapters.title: 🗃️ Memory hierarchy, storage and motherboard controllers
headings: Opening a file from an NVMe SSD
Interfaces are not the same as devices
chapters.text:
Distinguish fast volatile working memory, persistent storage, and the controllers that move data between them.
Static, volatile memory typically used for CPU caches and small on-chip buffers. Does not need DRAM-style refresh, but costs more area per bit.
Dense, volatile working memory requiring refresh. DDR generations specify interfaces; LPDDR is optimized for power-sensitive devices.
High-bandwidth memory for GPUs and accelerators. HBM stacks DRAM dies and uses wide interfaces; GDDR is a different high-bandwidth DRAM family.
Nonvolatile technologies. NAND supports dense mass storage; NOR and EEPROM are often used for firmware or configuration. Access granularity, endurance and erase behavior differ.
Application → syscall/VFS → filesystem → block layer → NVMe driver → PCIe → SSD controller → NAND flash; data returns to system DRAM, often with DMA, then is made available to the process. CPU cache lines are populated as code reads memory.
Controller distinction: a memory controller manages DRAM access; a storage controller manages device commands, queues and flash translation; a cache controller maintains cache state/coherence. The chipset/PCH can provide I/O connectivity but does not universally “control all traffic” in modern SoCs.
PCIe is a high-speed interconnect; NVMe is a storage command protocol commonly carried over PCIe; USB is a peripheral interconnect; Ethernet covers wired networking standards; I²C and SPI are serial buses for embedded peripherals. Thunderbolt and USB4 support additional tunneling/transport behaviors.
Power path: adapter/battery → regulators and PMIC → voltage rails → processor, memory, radio and peripherals. Clock sources, PLLs and timers coordinate timing; they do not replace software scheduling.

chapters.title: Open Source: Contributors, Institutions and the Software Supply Chain
headings: How an open-source component reaches a bank or telecom network
chapters.text:
Open-source software is a governance and production model that underpins the Internet, operating systems, programming languages, cloud infrastructure, databases, browsers, cybersecurity and AI tooling. Its success depends on maintainers, review, licensing, sustainable funding and deployment operators—not just public code repositories.
Collaborative software exchange predates the modern open-source label. Richard Stallman's GNU project (announced 1983) and the Free Software Foundation (1985) advanced software freedom and copyleft licensing. BSD UNIX traditions contributed networking and operating-system components. Linus Torvalds initiated the Linux kernel in 1991; GNU utilities and numerous independent projects helped form complete Linux-based operating environments. The Open Source Initiative formed in 1998 to promote a defined open-source licensing model.
Tim Berners-Lee and CERN made foundational Web technology broadly available; the IETF's open RFC process and W3C standards enabled interoperability. The Apache Software Foundation, Mozilla, Eclipse Foundation, Linux Foundation and Cloud Native Computing Foundation became important institutional homes for collaborative projects. Standards development and open-source implementation are related but different activities.
Contributors include individual volunteers, academic laboratories, corporate engineers, public-sector teams, nonprofits and foundation employees. Firms may fund projects because shared infrastructure reduces duplication, expands ecosystems, attracts developers or supports commercial services. Revenue can come from enterprise support, managed hosting, subscriptions, consulting, proprietary add-ons and hardware.
Open source does not automatically mean free hosting, unrestricted trademarks, absence of copyright, verified security or guaranteed maintenance. Licensing obligations, export restrictions, dependency provenance, vulnerability management and contributor governance matter in production.
A bank may run Linux on virtual machines, PostgreSQL for selected applications, OpenTelemetry for tracing and Kubernetes for orchestration, while using proprietary core-banking software and regulated payment networks. A telecom operator may run open-source network functions on commercial hardware, subject to interoperability, security and operational requirements. Open and proprietary components coexist.
Software bills of materials (SBOMs), reproducible builds, signed releases, dependency scanning, code review, least-privilege access and incident response are relevant to open-source supply-chain governance. An open repository provides inspectability, not automatic proof of safety. Procurement decisions should assess maintainer health, licenses, patch cadence and operational support.

chapters.title: Operating Systems, Kernel Boundaries & Hypervisor Architecture
headings: 1 · What an operating system actually contains
2 · Common OS services and the real execution path
3 · User space, kernel space and system calls
4 · Kernel architecture: monolithic is not “one large process”
5 · Hardware virtualization, guest OS and hypervisors
8 · VM versus container, with a practical example
9 · Walkthrough: request from browser to SSD and back
10 · Revision guide: source ideas and corrected formulations
chapters.text:
Original handwriting preserved unchanged; editorial corrections expanded into mechanisms, practical examples and verification steps.
Original idea: OS is the main software managing hardware resources; applications are user-specific; services and utilities run in the background; libraries and system files support both.
Precise model: An operating system is not only its kernel. A Linux distribution typically contains the Linux kernel, system libraries (such as glibc or musl), an init/service manager (often systemd), device-management tools, shells, utilities and optional graphical components. Applications may be user-facing or background services; a driver may execute in kernel space or user space, depending on the driver architecture.
Example: When an Nginx service receives an HTTPS request, Nginx is an application in user space, the TCP/IP stack and socket operations involve the kernel, the NIC driver interacts with network hardware, and systemd may supervise the Nginx process. The OS does not literally “manage everything”: firmware, hypervisors, hardware controllers and applications have their own responsibilities.
Verify: uname -r , ps -p 1 -o comm= , systemctl status nginx (when installed), lsmod , lspci -k .
Example: cat /var/log/app.log | grep ERROR involves process creation, pipe IPC, file descriptors, VFS, storage reads, memory mappings and scheduler decisions—multiple OS services cooperating.
Correction: “Kernel space does; user space asks” is a useful starting analogy, not a universal rule. User-space applications perform most computation directly on the CPU; the kernel is entered for privileged services, interrupts, exceptions and system calls. Userspace is not a separate CPU, and the kernel is not one giant ordinary user process.
Real example: A Python program computes sum(range(100000)) largely in user mode; opening a file crosses into kernel mode. A context switch between processes and a user-to-kernel mode transition are related but distinct events.
Verify: strace -e trace=openat,read,write cat /etc/hostname (if strace installed); inspect /proc/self/maps .
Original note: Linux has a monolithic kernel handling CPU, memory and drivers with a single large process.
Example: A userspace application invokes read() ; the kernel may execute VFS and filesystem code in that process's context, while separate kernel workers handle deferred work. The same kernel serves all ordinary processes in a Linux host.
Cross-link: This is essential for understanding containers: containers typically share the host Linux kernel but isolate selected resources with namespaces and cgroups.
Original idea: A hypervisor abstracts physical CPU, RAM, storage and networking so multiple VMs can run independently.
How it works: Each VM is presented virtual CPUs, guest physical memory, virtual devices and a virtual disk. The guest OS runs its own kernel. CPU virtualization uses processor support such as Intel VT-x or AMD-V; memory virtualization commonly uses second-level address translation (EPT/NPT); I/O may be emulated, paravirtualized (virtio) or passed through.
Example: A 16-core, 64-GB Linux server might host several KVM guests. Assigning 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM to a guest does not mean four physical cores are permanently dedicated; the host schedules vCPU threads. Overcommitment, NUMA locality, storage latency and ballooning affect performance.
Verify: lscpu | grep -i virtualization ; on a KVM host inspect virsh list --all and virsh dominfo <vm> .
Correction: “Type 1 always fastest; Type 2 always slower” is too absolute. Hardware acceleration, device virtualization, drivers, workload, scheduling and configuration dominate many practical results.
Real-world failure example: A single KVM host runs a billing VM. If its motherboard fails, the VM stops even though it was virtualized. With two or more properly configured hosts, quorum/fencing, replicated or shared storage and HA management, the VM may be restarted elsewhere. Restart is not zero-downtime: application recovery and storage consistency still matter.
AWS correction: An AWS Region is a geographic grouping of Availability Zones; an AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power/networking characteristics. An EC2 instance is a virtual server (or bare-metal option). A Region is not equivalent to a single hypervisor, and an AZ is not simply one data center.
Analogy only: Hypervisor = building's space allocator; cluster manager = campus-wide relocation coordinator; AZ = independently engineered site grouping. These are explanatory analogies, not technical identities.
Example: A KVM VM runs Ubuntu with its own kernel and an ext4 filesystem on a virtual disk. A Docker container inside that VM runs Nginx and shares the VM's kernel. Kubernetes schedules Pods onto nodes; it does not turn every container into a full VM.
Commands: docker inspect <container> to review namespace/network settings; lsns to inspect namespaces; systemd-cgls for cgroup hierarchy.
Why it matters: This one request connects the notes on OS services, scheduling, RAM, storage abstraction, networking and virtualization. In a VM there is another virtual-device/host layer; in a container the application usually uses the shared host kernel.

chapters.title: Packet switching, LANs and internetworking
headings: Who developed, funded, owned and operated the systems?
chapters.text:
Technology, infrastructure, network architecture, institutional ownership and business economics.
Packet switches, ARPANET IMPs, Ethernet, TCP/IP, UNIX, microprocessors, LAN adapters, routers, optical fiber, relational databases and PCs.
ARPA/DARPA, NSF, universities, telecom incumbents, IBM, Intel, Xerox, Cisco, Microsoft, Apple and standards organizations. These participants had different roles: research sponsorship, equipment supply, network operation, regulation, standardization and service consumption should not be conflated.
Circuit-switched carrier networks alongside packet-switched research networks; LANs joined through routers and common protocols.
Enterprise hardware, software licensing, leased data services, commercial networking and IT integration.
Packet switching divides traffic into independently forwarded units; TCP/IP enabled interconnection among heterogeneous networks without central ownership.
An office PC sends an Ethernet frame to a switch; a router forwards its IP packet toward a remote network. At each routed hop the link-layer framing may change while the IP-layer delivery objective persists.
Research funding, standards, vendors and carriers jointly enabled interoperable networking. ARPANET was not identical to the modern Internet.

chapters.title: Physical networks, Kubernetes networking and enterprise traffic paths
headings: 03 · ADC: network delivery, application delivery, and observability
04 · SAN, iSCSI, Fibre Channel and CSI
06 · Trace a packet: laptop to application Pod
chapters.text:
From modem and router to cluster datapaths, ingress, CNI, CSI, load balancers and the access–distribution–core design.
Technical correction policy: detailed mechanisms, examples and verification in the corrections handbook
B011-P04: Kubernetes equivalents for modem, firewall, router, switch, server NIC, physical media, VLAN, LAG. B011-P05: storage-area-network adapters and the application delivery controller (ADC). B011-P06: guided and unguided media, ISP-to-Wi-Fi traffic chain and device responsibilities. B011-P07: ordered roles of modem/ONT, edge router, firewall, core, distribution, access, endpoints and application security.
Editorial method: each original analogy is retained as a hypothesis, followed by the closest real implementation and limits. A CNI is a plugin interface, not itself a cable; a Kubernetes Service is a virtual service abstraction, not an Ethernet switch.
ISP network / last-mile fiber, DSL, or cellular │ [ONT / modem / cellular gateway] — terminates provider access technology │ Ethernet or integrated interface [Edge router] — L3 forwarding, default route, BGP or static routing, optional NAT │ [Firewall / security zones] — policy, stateful inspection, DMZ boundaries │ [Core switch pair] — resilient high-capacity campus backbone │ [Distribution switches] — aggregation, routing boundaries, ACLs as designed │ [Access switches] — endpoints, VLAN membership, PoE, Wi-Fi AP uplinks ├── [Wi-Fi AP] )))) laptops and phones ├── [Server NIC / HBA] — compute or storage fabrics └── [Industrial gateway] — OT/IoT segmentation Important qualification: this is a teaching topology, not a required universal sequence. Real designs may collapse core and distribution, place firewalls in different positions, or combine ONT/router/firewall/AP into one appliance. A router does not necessarily perform NAT; NAT is an independent function. Fiber optics carry modulated light rather than requiring a classic analog telephone modem.
Your note correctly separates network traffic (packets, TCP/UDP) from application traffic (HTTP/HTTPS requests) and monitoring. An application delivery controller may terminate TLS, perform L4/L7 load balancing, health checks, persistence, request routing and sometimes WAF protections. Modern implementations include dedicated appliances, software reverse proxies and cloud managed load balancers.
Client HTTPS request → public listener / ADC → TLS termination (optional) → policy + routing + health-based backend selection → backend pool: app-A | app-B | app-C → response via ADC or configured return path Observability: metrics + logs + traces + health checks Correction: DPDK is a userspace packet-processing framework, not a universal requirement for ADCs. ADCs can be built on ordinary kernel networking; eBPF, DPDK, ASICs or SmartNICs are optional acceleration choices.
The note maps iSCSI / Fibre Channel storage networks to CSI (Container Storage Interface) . They address different layers: iSCSI carries SCSI over TCP/IP; Fibre Channel provides a dedicated storage transport; HBAs connect hosts to storage fabrics. CSI is a standardized interface by which container orchestrators request provisioning, attachment and mounting through storage drivers.
Application in Pod → filesystem → PersistentVolumeClaim → Kubernetes CSI driver → storage provisioner → block/file storage backend → (possibly iSCSI / FC / NVMe-oF / NFS / cloud storage) → physical disks / SSDs Correction: CSI is not a SAN controller or a replacement for Fibre Channel. It integrates Kubernetes with whichever storage backend the CSI driver supports.
Guided: copper twisted pair, coaxial and fiber constrain signal propagation along a material path. Unguided: radio and other wireless electromagnetic propagation use space as the transmission medium. Virtual: VLANs, VRFs, tunnels, VXLAN overlays, veth pairs, Linux bridges, virtual switches, VPNs and software-defined policies are logical constructs implemented on physical hardware and links.
VLANs segment Layer-2 broadcast domains; VRFs isolate routing tables; VPNs can provide protected tunnels; VXLAN encapsulates L2 segments over an L3 underlay; LAG bonds links into one logical aggregation; SSIDs identify Wi-Fi networks, but SSIDs alone do not guarantee isolation.
Laptop app creates HTTPS request → OS TCP/IP stack → laptop Wi-Fi NIC → radio frames → AP → access switch → distribution/core → firewall → edge router → ISP → Internet → public load balancer → Gateway/Ingress → Service backend selection → worker-node NIC → CNI datapath → Pod eth0 → socket → application process At each hop, distinguish physical signal , link-layer framing , IP forwarding , transport connection , TLS security , and application request . A Service can use iptables, IPVS or eBPF depending on cluster configuration; not every packet necessarily passes through every named component.

chapters.title: 🧠 Processing engines, instruction sets and configurable logic
headings: RISC, CISC, ARM, x86 and RISC-V
chapters.text:
Processing hardware differs by programmability, data parallelism, latency, energy budget and the work it accelerates—not simply by being a “brain.”
An instruction set architecture specifies the software-visible machine interface: instructions, registers, exceptions and memory model. A microarchitecture is the internal implementation (pipelines, caches, predictors, execution units). RISC/CISC are broad historical design traditions, not reliable one-word predictions of energy use or speed.
x86-64 is used by Intel and AMD processors; Arm and RISC-V are distinct ISAs. An ASIC or FPGA can implement RISC or CISC CPU cores; these terms classify different design dimensions.
Source code → compiler/assembler → ISA machine instructions → OS loader → CPU fetch/decode/execute → cache and memory transactions → buses/interconnect → devices. An FPGA design instead uses RTL or higher-level hardware tools → synthesis → place-and-route → configuration bitstream → programmable logic.
Correction to a useful shorthand: an MCU runs firmware, but the firmware is not necessarily “stored in its memory” as a single undifferentiated region; flash, ROM, SRAM and external storage play different roles.

chapters.title: Public Infrastructure, Private Ecosystems and the Changing Geography of Control
headings: A layered history of authority—not a one-way privatization
chapters.text:
From chartered trade networks and regulated telecommunications to cloud platforms, open standards and AI.
From postal systems to cloud infrastructure, technical capabilities have been financed and governed through combinations of public agencies, private enterprises, state-owned companies, universities, nonprofit institutions and international bodies. Changes in ownership did not eliminate public regulation; they changed where investment, operations, interface control and economic rents were concentrated.
States financed research, allocated radio spectrum, built or regulated national communications, purchased early computing systems, operated postal networks and established legal conditions for international trade. Some assets were built by public enterprises; others were privately financed under public rights-of-way, licensing or procurement. Public contribution should not be mistaken for public ownership of every later commercial asset.
Telegraph networks crossing national borders faced incompatible procedures, tariffs and equipment conventions. The International Telegraph Union emerged in 1865 to coordinate international telegraph services. Standardization reduced transaction friction even while participating networks retained differing ownership arrangements. The business problem was not merely transmitting electricity; it was enabling messages and charges to cross jurisdictions predictably.
NSFNET supported academic networking and helped expand TCP/IP connectivity. As private providers built national networks, NSF-supported transition arrangements and network access points enabled interconnection. Retirement of the NSFNET backbone in 1995 did not create a single private owner of the Internet. It accelerated an ecosystem of independently administered networks, carriers, ISPs and exchange arrangements.
The U.S. Bell System was a historically important example of vertical integration. The 1984 divestiture separated AT&T local operating companies into regional groups. Competition and new markets expanded in some segments, while later mergers reconcentrated ownership. Market structure must therefore be studied dynamically: monopoly, regulated monopoly, oligopoly, contestable markets and competitive supply chains are distinct conditions.

chapters.title: Shared Foundations, Open Source and the Construction of Private Ecosystems
headings: 1. What counts as a public foundation?
4. Why large companies contribute to open source
chapters.text:
How public research, common standards and open software can become the foundations of privately differentiated products and platforms.
A technology firm can build a private business using resources it does not exclusively own: public scientific knowledge, roads and rights-of-way, radio spectrum administered by the state, university research, standards published by voluntary bodies, and open-source implementations. These are not interchangeable forms of “government-provided resources.” Spectrum is licensed or otherwise authorized, roads and rights-of-way are governed by law, publicly funded research has varying licensing conditions, and open-source code is distributed under its particular copyright license.
Consider an online retailer. It may use the publicly interconnected Internet, a privately owned access provider, Linux servers, an open-source database, a commercial cloud platform, privately owned fulfillment centers, and public roads for deliveries. Its advantage may lie in logistics, product selection, customer experience, data operations and contracts rather than ownership of the underlying Internet protocol.
Contributing upstream can reduce duplicated engineering, attract contributors, improve compatibility, distribute maintenance costs, influence technical direction and encourage adoption of a wider ecosystem. Firms may open-source an infrastructure layer while selling hosting, support, security, devices, analytics or enterprise features. Other firms may keep core intellectual property proprietary. Neither strategy is inherently universal or permanent.
Example — Kubernetes: Google originally developed Kubernetes and donated it to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Multiple companies now contribute to its development and sell managed Kubernetes services. The shared orchestration project enables competition at the infrastructure and service layer, but cloud-specific identity, networking and storage features can still increase migration costs.
Example — Linux: device makers, cloud providers and enterprise vendors all use the kernel. Some sell subscriptions and support; others use Linux inside proprietary devices or commercial cloud services. The kernel's openness does not automatically make all associated firmware, applications or service APIs open.

chapters.title: The Global Digital Industry Stack: India, United States, Europe and China
headings: 3. India: public digital rails and private innovation
4. United States: research networks, enterprise platforms and hyperscale services
5. European Union: market integration and platform governance
6. China: state direction and large-scale commercial ecosystems
chapters.text:
A layer-by-layer account of end-user delivery, government roles, private networks, payment systems and regional institutional models.
India's digital economy combines public-sector and private telecom operators, regulated banks, national payment infrastructure and commercial applications. UPI, operated by NPCI, enables interoperable payment initiation across participating financial institutions and applications. The public digital infrastructure model does not imply that every participant is government-owned or that banks cease to operate their own core systems. Private telecom carriers and cloud operators remain important delivery layers.
Example: A customer pays a small merchant through a mobile application. The phone reaches the Internet over a carrier network; the app and participating financial institutions exchange payment instructions through relevant payment infrastructure; bank accounts and settlement arrangements remain distinct from the mobile app's user interface. Network connectivity, authentication, payment authorization and settlement are separate failure domains.
Government and academic research contributed to internetworking, while private ISPs, hardware suppliers, software companies and cloud providers expanded commercial access and services. A modern business may use a private enterprise WAN, publicly reachable websites, cloud virtual networks, SaaS subscriptions and payment processors simultaneously. This creates a mixture of open standards, proprietary service contracts and regulated industry responsibilities.
European telecommunications developed through different national public and private models and later cross-border market coordination. The Digital Markets Act addresses designated gatekeepers and includes interoperability obligations for certain services and operating-system features. Regulation is not ownership: public authorities can influence access and competition without directly operating the platform.
China combines major state-owned telecom carriers with private and other commercially organized technology firms. Industrial policy, network regulation, domestic digital payments, e-commerce and cloud services shape an ecosystem whose institutional arrangement differs from the US and EU. Individual sectors should be assessed using documented ownership and current rules rather than treating all Chinese technology companies as state-owned.
A multinational may host an application in multiple cloud regions, use DNS-based routing and CDNs for end users, connect offices through SD-WAN overlays, and rely on local carriers for last-mile access. Its data residency, privacy, financial and telecommunications obligations can vary by jurisdiction. Cloud abstraction makes deployment programmable but does not remove dependence on physical facilities, international connectivity, legal entities and national law.
References support the institutional background and technical definitions. Interpretive comparisons and illustrative models are identified as analysis rather than established causal findings.

chapters.title: The Global Digital Industry Stack: Ownership, Architecture and Revenue
headings: A digital service is a coalition of independently operated systems
From physical servers to virtual business operations
chapters.text:
How public, private, nonprofit and regulated systems jointly deliver telecommunications, finance, cloud and AI services.
Regulation, standards, energy, security and physical infrastructure affect every stage. Illustrative path. Real traffic, payment authorization and settlement need not follow one linear physical route. A mobile purchase can depend on semiconductor manufacturers, phone vendors, mobile operating systems, licensed spectrum, towers, radio access networks, fiber backhaul, ISP routing, Internet exchanges, data centers, open-source software, cloud APIs, payment systems and financial regulation. These are not one network or one company. Each participant has distinct technical interfaces, ownership, revenue streams and failure responsibilities.
Early enterprises often purchased and operated dedicated computing assets. Time-sharing improved utilization; virtual memory separated program address spaces from physical memory; hypervisors abstracted hardware into guest machines; VLANs, VPNs, overlays and software-defined networks abstracted network connectivity; containers packaged isolated processes; cloud platforms automated provisioning, billing and orchestration. The physical infrastructure never disappeared. Virtualization changed the control plane and allocation model, not the need for silicon, electricity, cables and skilled operators.
UPI demonstrates layered coordination. RBI regulates payment systems, NPCI operates UPI, banks and payment service providers participate, and consumer-facing apps compete on usability and distribution. The underlying shared infrastructure is not identical to a single private wallet. This arrangement illustrates how public regulation, industry-operated shared systems and private digital services can coexist.
An industrial firm can connect PLCs and sensors over field buses and industrial Ethernet to supervisory systems, MES and ERP. Private networks may use VLANs, firewalls and edge gateways, while suppliers access portals through Internet APIs. A cloud analytics service may use Linux, containers and managed databases. The factory retains physical production assets; digitization changes monitoring, coordination and business responsiveness.
A person in a rural area may connect by mobile radio or local Wi-Fi to an access network. A carrier aggregates traffic onto fiber, microwave or satellite links, then routes it through interconnected networks. DNS locates service endpoints, TLS protects application communication, and a nearby CDN may deliver content without crossing an ocean. Remote regions still face differences in coverage, affordability, energy, capacity and policy; “global reach” does not imply universal access.
A fiber cut is a transport failure; a BGP route leak affects reachability; a cloud region incident affects compute and storage; a database outage affects transactions; an identity-provider outage affects login; a payment switch incident affects authorization. No single layer can guarantee end-to-end availability. Contractual SLAs, operational SLOs, incident response, redundancy and independent oversight are different forms of accountability.

chapters.title: Vertical, Horizontal and Platform Integration Across Technology Eras
headings: How organizations grow, plateau and decline
chapters.text:
How companies expand, consolidate, compete, decline and reorganize their infrastructure and business models.
Vertical: adjacent stages of a value chain. Horizontal: comparable activities or competitors. Neither guarantees monopoly. Vertical integration combines successive stages of a value chain, such as chip design, device manufacturing, operating system, application distribution and customer service. Horizontal integration combines comparable products, companies or markets at the same stage. Platform integration coordinates independent groups through common interfaces, rules, payments, identity and distribution. These strategies may coexist in one corporation.
A technology market can pass through experimentation, expansion, standardization, consolidation, maturity and partial displacement. These are patterns, not mandatory stages. Product decline can coexist with continued use: mainframes remain important in finance, copper still carries traffic, and Web 1.0-style static documents remain useful. New architectures often absorb old capabilities rather than eliminate them.
Early accounting systems processed records in batches. MRP coordinated manufacturing materials; MRP II expanded manufacturing planning; ERP integrated finance, procurement, inventory and HR. Client-server ERP relied on enterprise databases and LAN/WAN links. SaaS ERP shifted operations and upgrades toward the vendor. API-connected platforms then linked suppliers, payments, logistics and analytics. AI assistants may augment forecasting and user interaction, but transaction integrity and financial controls remain essential.
A firm may initially integrate hardware and software to ensure compatibility, then open APIs to attract partners. Later, rivals may compete at the application layer while infrastructure providers consolidate. Conversely, a platform may integrate vertically into chips, data centers or content to reduce dependency and control performance. Integration is not synonymous with monopoly: relevant market definition, substitutability, entry barriers and regulatory context determine competition outcomes.

Time-sharing, IBM virtual machines, hypervisors, x86 hardware virtualization, virtual memory, VLANs, VPNs, VXLAN, SDN/NFV, containers, Kubernetes, APIs, ERP and SaaS.
IBM, VMware, Linux/KVM community, cloud providers, enterprise IT teams, telecom equipment vendors and open-source foundations. These participants had different roles: research sponsorship, equipment supply, network operation, regulation, standardization and service consumption should not be conflated.
Physical servers host guest OS instances; overlays provide logical network segmentation; cloud control planes provision resources through APIs.
Capital equipment and licenses expanded into usage-based cloud, managed services, SaaS subscriptions and platform fees.
Virtualization abstracts resources but does not remove physical dependencies. Business-process digitization is organizational change, not the same technical mechanism as a hypervisor.
A retailer runs its ERP in VMs on shared hosts, uses a virtual network for segmentation, deploys web services in containers and purchases SaaS for HR. These are different abstractions serving different purposes.
The cost center moves from only procuring hardware toward contracts, capacity planning, identity management, usage governance and resilience engineering.

headings: Source repositories, binary repositories and virtual views
chapters.text:
How software moves from an artifact repository into VM disks or Kubernetes containers, and how communications move across motherboard and device interfaces.

A target VM retrieves a vendor installation archive into a download directory, extracts it into a temporary working directory, and runs an installation script that writes program binaries and configuration to a persistent installation directory. A separately attached and mounted block volume can isolate application data from the operating-system disk. The exact vendor installation paths and supported volume layout must be checked against the product version.
Download → verify checksum/signature → extract → install → configure → attach/mount data disk → validate service
Source page 2 is reproduced without edits, including original spelling, annotations and crossings-out.
A VM installation usually runs vendor-supported installers on the guest OS. A container deployment typically builds or obtains an OCI image, pushes it to a registry, and deploys Kubernetes resources using Helm charts. OCI images are not only for microservices; they can package monoliths and enterprise software too.
VM: archive → installer → filesystem/service. Kubernetes: image → registry → image pull → Pod → Service
Source page 3 is reproduced without edits, including original spelling, annotations and crossings-out.
Generic repositories store arbitrary distributable archives such as ZIP, TAR.GZ, JAR and installation bundles. OCI-compatible repositories distribute container images and manifests. Artifactory can use supported external storage backends; it is not restricted to the VM local disk. Internal DNS, ingress, proxies, TLS and firewall policies determine how clients reach it.
Generic artifact: curl/wget + checksums. OCI artifact: docker/podman/containerd pull by tag or immutable digest.
Source page 4 is reproduced without edits, including original spelling, annotations and crossings-out.
Host VM IP, container/pod IP, Service IP and load-balancer IP are different addressing concepts. Multiple repositories can share one Artifactory server hostname while being distinguished by paths and repository keys. Container network addresses depend on the runtime and deployment mode; a container does not inherently use the host IP.
Client → DNS → TLS endpoint / reverse proxy → Artifactory repository path → binary or image layers
Source page 5 is reproduced without edits, including original spelling, annotations and crossings-out.
GitHub and GitLab primarily host versioned source and related development workflows. Artifactory stores and serves built artifacts. Local repositories hold managed artifacts; remote repositories cache upstream artifacts; virtual repositories expose a consolidated access endpoint. Repository authorization and TLS server identity are distinct from network address and DNS.
Source commit → CI build → test/sign/SBOM → binary artifact → repository → deployment
Source page 6 is reproduced without edits, including original spelling, annotations and crossings-out.
UART is asynchronous serial; USART can support synchronous and asynchronous modes. USB is a host/device-oriented serial bus with enumeration and protocol layers. GPIO is general-purpose signaling, not a protocol. I²C commonly uses SDA/SCL and addressed peripheral communication; SPI commonly uses clock, data lines and chip select; CAN is a robust shared communication bus. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and NFC are wireless technologies; MQTT is an application-layer publish/subscribe messaging protocol often carried over TCP/IP.
CPU/MCU → controller/driver → UART / I²C / SPI / CAN / USB → peripheral; sensor → network → MQTT broker → subscriber
Do not equate artifact repository with local-only storage, OCI with microservices only, container IP with host IP, virtual repository with physical copies, or MQTT with a radio protocol.
